                                   CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee observes that this Department is involved in examining new 
legislations for different Minis tries/Departments and also for repealing of obsolete laws. The 
Committee in its 101
st Report on Demands for Grants (2020-21) had made observations w ith 
regard to drafting errors and ambiguity in law/statutes and des ired for pre-legislative 
consultation and periodic review of legislations.  The Committe e is of the view that 
legislation enacted are not able to keep pace with changing soc io-economic developments 
leading to excessive litigations, financial loss to exchequer, disconnect with social milieu and 
so forth. (Para 3.15) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.15, it is to mention that:  
i. The process of legislation involves the study of social and financial costs, benefits and 
the key challenges that required to be settled before undertaki ng the legislations. The 
administrative Ministry/Department also identifies the problems  in the policy that 
needs to be addressed, the options it has considered and the re asons thereof in 
bringing forward a legislation.  
ii. Further, the Chapter 9 of the Manual of Parliamentary Procedure  in the Government 
of India (relating to legislation) provides that the concerned Ministry/Department has 
to formulate the legislative proposals in consultation with the  interested persons and 
authorities concerned, including holding discussions on the nec essity for the proposed 
legislation and on all matters of substance to be embodied therein. 
iii. Moreover, as per the Government of India (Allocation of Busines s) Rules, 1961, 
different subject matter or policies are allocated to different Ministries/Departments of 
the Government of India. Accordingly, the Ministries/Department s concerned with 
the subject matter initiates pre-legislative Consultations, hol ds deliberations with the 
public and all stakeholders and on that basis, finalise its leg islative policy and 
subsequently conduct the impact assessment after the legislations is enacted.  
iv. It is further pertinent to mention here that the Legislative De partment prepares draft 
laws in consultation with the administrative Ministry concerned  in accordance with 
the procedure laid down in the Manual of Parliamentary Procedur es, ordinarily within 
thirty days from the date of receipt of the proposal and after clearance from the 
Department of Legal Affairs. The refore, the Legislative Departm ent is merely a 
service provider Department catering its drafting services to t he 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India.  
 
Further Observation 
1.2 The Committee notes the Reply of the Department.  
8

                                  CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE 
GOVERNMENT             
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The Committee desires that a general consensus is required on the issue of Legislative 
Impact Assessment (LIA), and accordingly of the considered view that there has to be a nodal 
Ministry/Department for dealing with the issues related to LIA,  and believes that the 
Legislative Department, due to its expertise in legislative/cab inet note drafting is the most 
suitable Department under the Government of India for the purpo se. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Department to prepare a white paper  on the Legislative Impact 
Assessment in the country by taking learning experiences of oth er developed countries. (Para 
3.16) 
Action Taken 
2.1 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.16, it is to mention that:  
i. The Legislative Impact Assessment or Analysis is a transparent and informed process 
with the participation and involvement of all stakeholders so that the preparedness and 
availability of requisite administrative, financial and infrast ructural support for 
successful implementation of intended legislation is known befo re hand and the 
desired object can be achieved. 
ii. The Legislative Impact Assessment is wide enough to encompass w ithin its scope 
Judicial Impact Assessment, Social Impact Assessment, Financial Impact Assessment, 
Environment Impact Assessment, Employment Impact Assessment, etc.  
 Judicial Impact Assessment  helps in preserving Courts ability to keep pace 
with growing workload, ensures, adequate funding of Courts and improves 
administration of justice. 
 Social Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the socio-economic impact of 
legislation on people, particularly those from the economically  weaker section 
and marginalized section of society. 
 Financial Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the economic costs of 
proposed legislation.  
 Environment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating the beneficial and 
adverse impact of new legislation on environment, optimization of natural 
resources, reducing or mitigating potential negative impacts an d achieving 
9

sustainable development.  
 Employment Impact Assessment  helps in evaluating employment creation 
through proposed legislation. 
iii. A law is reviewed by the concerned Ministry/Department for exam ining its 
effectiveness and setting right m ischief, if any, created by su ch law on the basis of 
feedback, if any, received from the stakeholders and the other concerned persons, the 
data, if any, collected in this behalf, the comments/suggestion s, if any, received from 
the public, etc. Thereafter, the concerned Ministry/Department takes up necessary 
l e g i s l a t i v e  a c t i o n  e i t h e r  f o r  a m e n d m e n t  o r  r e p e a l  o f  t h e  l a w .  Post-enactment 
legislative impact assessment is also done by the Law Commissio n of India or such 
other body or commission set up specifically for such purpose, which is normally 
limited to the specific terms of reference. 
iv. Under the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1 961, each 
Ministry/Department has been allocated subject matters on which  t h a t  
Ministry/Department initiates, possess and implements legislati ve proposals and also 
studies social, economic, environmental and judicial impact of such  legislative 
proposals. 
v. In view of the above, pre-legislative consultations, legislative impact assessment /post 
legislation consultation are within the domain of the concerned  Ministry/Department. 
Hence, the pre and post Legislative Impact Assessment should be  done by the 
concerned Ministry/Department which piloted the legislation. Th erefore, the subject 
matter relating to legislative impact assessment does not come under the purview of 
the allocation of work to Legislative-I Section of this Department. 
vi. However, the Committee is of view that there has to be a nodal Ministry/Department 
for dealing with the issue related to Legislative Impact Assess ment and believes that 
the Legislative Department possess the expertise in legislative /cabinet note drafting 
and therefore, Legislative Department is considered as most sui table Department for 
the purpose. In this regards, it is to state that as explained above the legislative impact 
assessment /post legislation consultation is a wide concept and  involves intricacies, 
specialized knowledge, expertise, manpower, research work and i nfrastructure and as 
the Legislative Department does not intervene in the policy mat ter of the legislation 
rather only provides its drafting services to the Ministries/De partments. In view of the 
a b o v e ,  L e g i s l a t i v e  D e p a r t m e n t  i s  e x a m i n i n g  v a r i o u s  a s p e c t s  r e l ating to the 
recommendation made by the Department related Parliamentary Sta nding Committee, 
and the manner of its implementation and suitable decision take n by the competent 
authority will be communicated in due course of time. 
 
Further Observation 
 
2.2 The committee acknowledges the reply of the department.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH COMMITTEE

Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Committee observes that allocation to the Official Lang uage Wing (OLW) has 
marginally increased from the Financial Year (2020-21) to (2021 -22), except in the

remained constant in the current and preceding financial year, except allocation of Rs. 1.00 
crore (14.28 percent) increased in the forthcoming financial ye ar. These wings of the 
Department play a very important and significant role in transl ation of Central Acts, 
Ordinances and Subordinate legislation in Hindi and other Eight  Scheduled languages, and 
also in translation of judgements of Supreme Court and High Courts in Hindi.  (Para 2.7) 
3 . 1  I n  v i e w  o f  t h e  a b o v e ,  t h e  C o m m i t t e e  f e e l s  t h a t  t h e  s t a t i c  allocations made to these

Department.

3.8 The Committee notes the reply of the Department with regard  to initiation of the 
recruitment process to fill-up the vacancy positions in Vidhi S ahitya Prakashan. In this 
regard, the Committee reiterates its suggestions made in its ea rlier reports wherein the 
Committee had suggested expeditin g the process of finalization of amendments to 
recruitment rules and filling-up vacancies in consultation with  the concerned cadre 
controlling and recruiting authorities'. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.9 The Committee observes wide fluctuations in allocation unde r the various heads of 
election expenses over the years in BE & RE. It is also observe d that allocations for 
‘Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs)’ and ‘EVMs Professional  Services’ has been 
drastically reduced in BE (2022-23 ) over the projections made t o the Ministry of Finance. 
Further, the Committee is not satisfied with the rationale furn ished by the Department/ECI 
that the allocations under the Revenue head in BE (2022-23) for  electoral expenses will not 
adversely affect the work of the Department as audit certificat es takes around 2-3 years. If 
this was the rationale, then the Committee couldn’t fathom as t o why projection of Rs 
12

1594.60 crore for ‘Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs) was m ade to the Ministry of 
Finance initially. (Para 2.11) 
3.10 The Committee feels that reductions in allocations under t he head may be due to 
inaccurate projection or inflation of funds required and thereb y, failure of the 
Department/ECI to justify its projection to the Ministry of Fin ance. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that while making projections to the Mi nistry of Finance in future, 
the Department should ensure that its projection are rational a nd appropriate to meet its 
requirements. (Para 2.12) 
 
Action Taken 
3.11 (In response to Para 2.11),  it may be stated that the largest decrease is under Election 
head (conduct of elections) i.e. from projections made to Minis try of Finance (MOF) of Rs. 
1594.60 crore  [projected on the basis of B.E(2021-22) Rs.164.30 crore and R.E(2021-22) 
Rs.1572.80 crore ] to B.E.(2022-23) Rs.292.00 crore.   On account of Election related 
expenditure in the years 2021-22, this Department had received Audit Certificates from 8 
State Governments (Telangana, Uttarakhand, Tripura, Sikkim, Raj asthan, Himachal Pradesh, 
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh).  After the settlement of election accounts, projections of Rs.1400.00 
crore in R.E(2021-22) stage was made. MOF provided the requeste d amount in R.E stage 
through 2 nd Batch of Supplementary for the year 2021-22 and the same amoun t has been 
reduced in B.E(2022-23) and provided Rs. 292.00 Crore for Elect ion related expenditure.  
Further, releases would be made to the State Governments only a fter receipt of the valid 
Audit Certificates from the concerned Accountant General (AG) o ffices of the State 
Governments, which generally takes some time (2 to 3 years).  F urther, the Department has 
received audit certificates of 7 major states i.e. Andhra Prade sh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Tamilnadu, Bihar, Gujarat and Maharashtra and need of funds for  releases has been 
demanded at R.E(2022-23) stage. 
3.12 Recommendation made by the Committee (in Para 2.12) has be en noted down by the 
Department for future compliance  
Further observation 
 
3.13 The Committee observes that the Department is repeating th e same reply again, 
which is not acceptable to it. The Committee desires that herei nafter Department may 
make rational projections of its requirements. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.14 The Committee observes that posts in the Department are va cant due to various 
reasons, and feels that the Department needs to wholeheartedly pursue the issue with various 
authorities engaged in recruiting and posting of staff to fill- up the vacant positions. Further, 
13

the Committee feels that recruitment process may be initiated i n advance in anticipation of 
likely retirement/vacancy positions to avoid delays and, recomm ends that the Department 
should forward details of vacancy/anticipated vacancy positions  in advance to the 
recruiting/cadre controlling authorities. (Para 3.4) 
 
Action Taken 
 
Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP): 
 
3.15 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.4, VSP ha s submitted that they are 
taking the necessary action to fill up all vacant posts as reco mmended by the Committee to 
strengthen the VSP. Two vacant posts of Sub-Editors have been f illed up. The vacancies of 
Assistant (General), Lower Division Clerk (LDC) and Multitaskin g Staff (MTS) have been 
reported to Staff Selection Commission (SSC) for making recruit ment against these 
vacancies. VSP is continuously following up with SSC to expedit e the recruitment against 
these posts. Proposal for filling up one post of Editor on prom otion basis has already been 
sent to UPSC and VSP is following up with UPSC for expediting t he same.  The Ministry is 
taking up the matter with Deptt. of Personnel & Training for po sting of officials against the 
vacancies of  CSSS and CSS cadre posts. As regards the posts wh ich have been deemed 
abolished, a proposal for their revival is being sent to Department of Expenditure. 
 
Official Language Wing (OLW): 
 
3.16 As regards the Committee’s observation in Para 3.4, OLW ha s submitted that the total 
sanctioned staff strength of the OLW is 154. Out of this total staff strength, presently 96 posts 
are filled up and 58 posts are vacant. It is stated that maximu m vacant posts are from cadre of 
Regional Languages posts and the amendment in recruitment rules  for the post of Additional 
Legislative Counsel (Regional Languages), Deputy Legislative Co unsel (Regional 
Languages) and Assistant Legislative Counsel (Regional Language s) is under process. 
Further, it has now been decided that the vacant post of Region al Languages Officers may be 
filled through existing recruitment rules and action for fillin g up the same is under process. 
OLW has also approached the recruitment agencies to fill up the ir posts as early as possible. 
Status of action taken for filling up these vacancies is enclosed as Annexure-I
. 
 
Further Observation 
 
3.17 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. Further, the Committee 
recommends the Department may expedite the consultation process  with recruitment 
and cadre controlling agencies. 
 
3.18 In Official Language Wing(OLW), the Committee observes tha t posts in the 
Department are vacant due to various reasons. Some of the posts  like that of Deputy 
and Assistant Legislative Counsel (Regional Languages) are vacant since 2016 and most 
of the vacancies have been lying vacant since 2018. The Committ ee also observed that 
14

most of the vacancies have been reported to either SSC or are u n d e r  p r o c e s s .  I n  t h i s  
regard, the Committee feels that the vacancies have not been fi lled for extended period 
and therefore, recommends that a time frame should be decided w ith in which the 
recruitment process should be completed. The Committee may be a pprised the reasons 
for delay in filling up the vacant posts and corrective action may be taken in this regard. 
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
3.19 The Committee in its previous reports, including 101
st a n d  1 0 7th, on Demands for 
Grants had expressed its anguish over the lukewarm approach of the Department with regard 
to translation of Constitution and Central Government Acts in S cheduled Languages. The 
Committee observes that no noticeable improvement in the translation work has been made in 
Scheduled Languages or updation work of Constitution of India i n some Scheduled 
Languages, like Odia and Sanskrit language. The Committee wishe s to point out that it was 
last undertaken around 35-40 years ago. In this way, the Depart ment is not doing justice to 
these Scheduled languages. The Committee feels priority should be accorded for 
translating/updating Constitution of India and other Central Ac ts in Odia and Sanskrit at the 
earliest. (Para 3.10) 
3.20 The Committee also doesn’t agree with the rationale of the  Department that the 
process of translation is slow due to ongoing Covid-19 pandemic  situation as it observes that 
as on date, the Constitution of India has been translated only in 16 Scheduled Languages and 
further translation/updation work in scheduled language are pen ding for decades. The 
Committee feels that, instead of blaming the Covid-19 pandemic,  which is a recent 
phenomenon, the Legislative Department needs to improve its org anisational efficiency and 
get the Constitution of India translated/updated in all the reg ional languages without further 
delay.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department t o fix a timeframe for 
completing the translation/upda tion of Constitution of India in  all the scheduled languages 
and apprise this Committee in this regard while furnishing the Action Taken Replies. (Para 
3.11) 
Action Taken 
3.21 With reference to the Committee’s observation in Para No.3 .10 and 3.11, Regional 
Language Unit of Official Language Wing (OLW) has submitted tha t they are continuously 
striving to translate, update and publish of the Constitution o f India and all the Central Acts 
in all the languages as mentioned in the 8 th Schedule to the Constitution of India.  The 
Constitution of India has been translated and uploaded in 17 la nguages and it is updated in 9 
languages i.e Bengali, Dogri, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punj abi, Tamil, Telugu and 
15

Urdu.  It is under process of publication in Manipuri Meitei Sc ript.  Initiative is underway to 
entrust the work of translation, updation and printing of the Constitution of India in Assamese, 
Bodo, Gujarati, Konkani, Kashmiri, Maithili, Nepali, Odia, Sant ali, Sanskrit and Sindhi 
through the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL establi shed under the Ministry of 
Education, Government of India).  The Department is expediting to translation and 
publication of the Constitution of India at the earliest and al l central Acts in the region 
languages. 
Further Observation 
 
3.22 The Committee acknowledges the initiatives of the Departme nt. The committee 
reiterates its recommendations made in its previous Reports viz . 96 th, 101 st and 114 th 
Report to bring out publication of the Constitution of India in  a l l  t h e  S c h e d u l e d  
languages of the Constitution. Further, the Committee would lik e to know about the  
initiatives taken for the translation, updation and printing of  the Constitution of India 
in Assamese, Bodo, Gujarati, Konkani, Kashmiri, Maithili, Nepal i, Odia, Santhali, 
Sanskrit and Sindhi and the current status of the such initiati ves may be forwarded for

Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.23 The Committee also observes that posts of language officer  are vacant for Assamese, 
Gujarati, Kanada, Odia, Urdu, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Konkani, Nepali  and Manipuri. Further, no 
post of language officers have been sanctioned for Bodo, Santha li, Maithali, Dogri and 
Kashmiri languages. The Committee is surprised to note that no post/s for language officers 
has been created in the Department for Kashmiri language (1950) , which was included in the 
Eighth Schedule more than 70 years ago. Further, even after 17 years of inclusion in the Eight 
Schedule, no posts of languages o fficers have been created for Bodo, Santhali, Maithali,  and 
Dogri, despite having large number of people speaking these Sch eduled Languages viz. 
Maithali ( 12,179,122), Santhali (6,469,600), Kashmiri (5,527,6 98), Dogri (2,282,589), and 
Bodo (1,350,478). The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department not only to fill-
up the vacant position of language officers in the Department  and also approach appropriate 
authorities for creating posts of language officers for Bodo, S anthali, Maithali, Dogri and 
Kasmiri languages without any further delay. (Para 3.12) 
Action Taken

(OLW) has submitted that the recruitment rules for the post of Group ‘A’ Officer (Regional

Maithali, Dogri and Kasmiri languages. As per records, there is  already a sanctioned post for 
16

the Santhali language. It is submitted that necessary action wi ll be taken up with the 
concerned authorities for getting sanctioned posts for these fo ur languages viz. Bodo, 
Maithali, Dogri and Kasmiri. 
 
Further Observation

action may be initiated for getting posts of the four language viz. Bodo, Maithali, Dogri 
and Kashmiri filled. The Department may apprise the Committee o f the action taken in 
this regard.

ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.0 The Committee observes that as against an allocation of Rs.  253.00 crore in the 
current Financial Year, the expenditure of the ECI till 31
st January, 2022 is only Rs. 158.74 
crore (63 percent approx.). The Committee observes that out of the total allocation of Rs. 
7.00 crore for capital expenditure in the current financial yea r; the ECI has not been able to 
spend a single rupee till 31 st January, 2022. The Committee understands that expenditure 
under the capital head is directly linked with the external age ncies like CPWD and NBCC for 
construction of building for ECI at Dwarka, however, the Committee  fails to understand why 
only Rs. 158.74 has been spent under the Revenue head which is well within the control of 
ECI, and accordingly, the Committee recommends ECI to furnish c ogent reasons for under-
utilisation of funds allocated to it under the Revenue head. (Para 2.17) 
     
4.1 The Committee also observes allocations have been reduced u nder Revenue heads- 
Information Technology, Voters’ Awareness, and Training of ECI,  w h i c h  t h e  C o m m i t t e e  
believes are important components of electoral processes. The Committee feels that reduction 
in allocations under the Revenue Expenditure for the forthcomin g financial year vis-à-vis 
projection to the Ministry of Finance may be due to the inabili ty of the ECI to spend the 
allocations made for various heads in the current financial year. (Para 2.18) 
 
4.2 The Committee, accordingly, recommends the ECI to improve i ts spending capacity 
on various activities, as non- expe nditure of amount allocated reflects under-performance of 
activities/under-utilisation of resources. The Committee is the refore of the view that an 
important institution like ECI should not be forced to limit it s activities due to financial 
constraints and recommends the Department/ECI to approach the M inistry of Finance for 
enhanced allocation during the RE stage, especially for Informa tion Technology and Voters’ 
Awareness and Training . (Para 2.19) 
 
VACANCY POSITION IN ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
4.3 The Committee is of the view that shortage of secretarial s taff may adversely affect its 
functioning at optimal level, and accordingly, recommends that the ECI should pursue the 
matter with the cadre controlling and recruiting agencies to fi ll-up these vacancies in a time 
bound manner. (Para 3.20) 
18

 
4.4 The Committee takes note of the Constitutional provisions a nd also the submission by 
the Election Commission of India that Regional Commissioner/s m ay be appointed by the 
President of India if required; however, after the first Genera l Election, they were not 
appointed. The Committee is of the view that ECI should have op timal level of manpower as 
per its requirements and accordingly, recommends the Legislativ e Department/Election 
Commission of India to submit its views on the appointment of R egional Commissioner/s for 
the forthcoming General Elections to the Lok Sabha in the year 2024. (Para 3.21) 
VOTERS' REGISTRATION AND AWARENESS 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.5 The Committee appreciates the ECI for achieving optimal lev el of voter’s enrolment 
in the electoral roll as it had already registered 95 crore vot ers in the country. The Committee 
also takes note of the initiatives of the ECI for augmenting IT  infrastructure to facilitate 
electoral processes, and believes that with the optimal utilisa tion of modern information and 
communication and technologies it would be able to overcome the  geographical and physical 
limitations.  The Committee feels that along with the voters’ e nrolment in the electoral roll, 
the ECI may also explore the feasibility of  conducting post-po ll exercise affecting 
participation of voters’  and reasons for low voters’ turnout o n the day of election as an 
academic activity to improve its performance in future elections. (Para 3.24) 
 
COMMON ELECTORAL ROLL 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.6 The Committee in its previous reports had recommended the D epartment/ECI for a 
Common Electoral Roll from Parliamentary to local body election s, and accordingly, 
appreciates the Department/ECI f or sensitizing the Government i n bringing the Election 
Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 to provide multiple qualifying dates  for preparation and 
revision of electoral roll, thereby, encouraging the States to adopt the Common Electoral 
R o l l s .  T h e  C o m m i t t e e  i s  o f  t h e  v i e w  t h a t  s i n c e  t h e  r e l e v a n t  s t atutes have already been 
amended, the Department/ECI may pursue with the remaining State  Governments/UTs to 
implement the common electoral roll. (Para 3.31)

Commission of India (ECI). Accordingly, ECI has been requested to provide the statement of

the paras 2.17, 2.18, 2.19, 3.20, 3.21, 3.24 and 3.31 from the Legislative 
Department/Election Commission. The Committee also found that s imilar observations

VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.5 The Committee further observes  that the distribution of notaries across the States/UTs is 
uneven and believes that there should be objective criteria to project required number of notaries 

 
10 
in States/UTs to optimally utilize their services. The Committee understands that notary -ship is 
not a civil post or any kind of employment under the Central Government and hence does not 
attract any affirmative policy in any manner. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the 
Department to make a wholehearted endeavour so that composition of notaries is inc lusive and 
reflects the balanced socio-economic composition of the society. (3.15) 
Action Taken 
1.6 In terms of provisions of Notaries Rules, 1956, only relaxations in terms of „ experience 
as an advocate/legal practitioner „ as eligibility condition are provided in favour of social 
category candidates  (SC/ST/OBC/Women/PH) ( seven years‟ experience vis a vis 10 years for 
general category candidates) . The prescribing of eligibility qualifications in terms of experience 
however do not mean any kind of social category reservations as such in favour of any of these 
categories in appointment of notaries.  
1.7 The schedule appended to the Notaries rules, 1956 provide details of maximum number 
of notaries to be appointed in the State/UT by the central Government as well as State 
Governments. The schedule is periodically amended in view of request made by the re spective 
State Governments for enhancement of their State/UT quota and same is considered on the 
criteria of (i) increase in the population of the concerned State/UT (ii) increase in the number of 
districts or tehsil or taluka of concerned State/UT. 
1.8 The central Government also enhance their quota for central government notaries on 
account of increase in number of Courts/Tribunals, creation of more districts /Talukas, increase 
in commercial activities in the State, industrialization, increase in number o f educational 
institutions and increase in population in the State. 
1.9 Accordingly, vacancies for notaries in particular State/UTs are determined on account of 
number of factors explained above. 
Further Observation 
 
1.10 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
 
DIGITAL SIGNATURES FOR AUTHENTICATION OF NOTARIZED DOCUMENTS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.11 The Committee in its previous reports, including 101st, 107th and 109th Reports dealt the 
issue of digital signatures and had recommended the Department t o explore the feasibility of 
introducing Digital Signatures for authenticating notarized documents to reduce malpractices of 
anti-dating or/and attestation of blank document, etc. and improve transparency. The Committee 
also feels that along with digital s ignatures, the Department may also explore the feasibility of 

 
11 
introducing e -affidavits as practice of e -stamping is already in vogue and the Government of 
India is also promoting courts through video conferencing and virtual courts. (3.16) 
Action Taken 
 
1.12 The issue of introduction of digital signature facility for notary attestations has been 
examined. It is submitted that majority of the documents which are presented for notarization 
before a Notary Public are invariably in the physical form. Apart from  signature, a notary has to 
put his seal and also affix notarial stamp on the documents being notarized by him. Digital 
signature means „authentication of any electronic record by a subscriber by means of any 
electronic method or procedure on the documents ‟. Using of digital signature for authentication 
of documents to be notarized by a Notary, such documents must be in electronic form whereas 
majority of such documents are invariably presented in physical form which are not compatible 
for Digital Signature. 
  
1.13 As regards introducing e -affidavits, the subject is not within the purview of the Notaries 
Act 1952 and rules framed thereunder.  
  
1.14 Thus, in present circumstances introducing digital signatures for authentication of 
documents on the part of Notary may not be viable. 
 
Further Observation 
 
1.15 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
 
EMPANELMENT OF COUNSELS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.16 The Committee observes that the Department has not devised any criteria/methodology to 
project the required number of panel counsels for a Court/ Tribunal. Further, there is no 
information available on the Department‟s website with regard to empanelment process of panel 
counsels. The Committee, accordingly, feels that the Department needs to devise a ra tional 
methodology for projecting required number of panel counsels/advocates based on the number of 
institution/pending cases, nature of cases and so forth to ensure transparency and optimal 
utilisation of government resources. The details of empanelment process/criteria also need to be 
uploaded in the Department‟s website for the benefit of potential candidates applying for 
empanelment as government/panel counsels. (3.19) 
Action Taken 
1.17 It is stated that the panel counsel for various courts / tribunals  are engaged by this 
Department to represent Union of India for a particular term and as such they are not appointed 
against any civil post. Therefore, the concept of sanctioned post or vacant posts does not apply in 

 
12 
case of panel counsel. Presently, there  is no criteria/methodology to project the required number 
of panel counsel for a court/tribunal. It is pertinent to mention here that relationship between a 
panel counsel & Government is that of an Advocate and client. Empanelment/engagement of 
Advocates to represent Government before various courts should not be compared with 
appointment to a “post” in the Government. There is no extra financial burden on the 
Government on empanelling large number of counsel as payment of fee is paid to them on case -
to-case basis in lieu of their professional services. Further, Government has more choices to 
choose/select suitable counsel from the panel in terms of expertise and experience required to 
defend a particular case.   However, keeping in view the size of the cour t, number of Central 
Govt. litigations etc. appropriate number of counsel are engaged for that court. Moreover, due to 
expiry of terms, deaths and resignation etc. of counsel, the process of empanelment/engagement 
of Advocates as panel counsel is an ongoin g process due to which projecting total number of 
panel counsel for a High Court on an earlier date is not feasible.   
1.18 Further, it is a settled proposition of law enunciated by the Hon‟ble Supreme Court of 
India and various High Courts that Government  Advocate being a special engagement has no 
vested right to continue in that position. Appointment of Government Advocate is purely a 
prerogative of the Government because it is a professional engagement between a litigant and its 
Advocate. As such, at pre sent, Advocates are empanelled / engaged by this Department for all 
courts/tribunals in the country with the approval of Hon‟ble Minister for Law & Justice and 
orders in this regard are issued on behalf of the President.   We may, therefore, publish this 
procedure on website of the Department for public information.  
Further Observation 
 
1.19 The Committee takes note of the reply.

BUDGET ALLOCATION TO INDIAN LAW INSTITUTE 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Department/ ILI  has informed that over the last 5 years, 100 percent of funds 
released to ILI have been utilised and there was excess expenditure (50 percent approx.) of ILI 
vis-à-vis grants allocated for the same period. The ILI has informed this Committee that it has 
incurred an expenditure of Rs. 6.7 crore in the current financial year (as on 31.1.2022) towards 
payment of salaries and allowances. However, the Committee observes that the ILI is not able to 
meet even its salary requirement for teaching and non -teaching staff from the grants allocated by 
the Department of Legal Affairs. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that ILI being a 
grantee institution should not eternally depend on government grants and thus it needs to become 
self sufficient to meet its basic r equirements. The Committee also feels that for the time being, 
grants-in-aid to ILI may be enhanced. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department 
to at least provide grants -in-aid to meet its 100 percent salary and allowances expenditure for 
sanctioned positions for the next five years. (2.13) 
3.1 The Committee observes that majority of earnings of ILI is from course fee charged from 
students/trainees, rent received from Ministry of Law and Justice for leasing its premises, and 
interests. The Committee also observes that the pattern of earning has remained same for the last 
2-3 years, except some variations in financial year 2020 -21 due to Covid -19 pandemic. The 
Committee is of the view that the ILI being a research Institution, needs to generate mo re and 
more funds from academic and consultancy activities, which are its core activities and not from 
rent/leasing its premises to Ministries/Departments of Government of India. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the ILI to explore additional avenues to generate more funds from 
research/ consulting activities and gradually become self sufficient. (2.14) 
 
3.2 The Committee also feels that ILI needs to expand its activities by way of introducing 
demand degrees/diploma programmes and consultancy activitie s by optimally utilising its 
existing infrastructure and accordingly, is of the view that its premises rented out to the 
Departments/institutions needs to be utilised for its own expansion. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Department to get the ILI premises vacated for its expansion. (2.15) 
Action Taken  
3.3 The Department is providing almost 50% of total salary and allowances expenditure of 
Indian Law Institute (ILI) as Grants -in-Aid. Besides that Rs.6.50 crore has been provided to ILI 

 
25 
in the RE-2021-22 as one time special Grants -in-Aid for payment of outstanding property tax to 
NDMC and for strengthening of building infrastructure. During Revised Estimate (2021 -22), the 
Department allocated Rs. 3.00 crore and the same allocation has been retai ned for BE- 2022-23. 
Keeping in view the recommendation of the Committee to enhance the allocation for salary and 
allowances, the proposal for enhancement of Grant -in-Aid (Salary) to Rs.6.00 crore has been 
agreed to by this Department and sent to Integrate d Finance Division for getting the same 
approved by the Competent Authority. 
3.4 ILI has informed that at present, the Institute manages to generate an amount of Rs.4.00 
crore through its own resources i.e. course fee, rent, sale of publications, research activities etc. 
Further, it is difficult for the Institute to introduce more academic courses due to space 
constraints and lack of infrastructure and there is very less scope for the Institute to earn more 
revenue from its core activities. However, the Ins titute is continuously striving to explore more 
avenues for expansion of its academic, research and consulting activities to generate more funds. 
3.5 The Indian Law Institute (ILI) building has been constructed with a loan from the 
Government with an agreement between the Government and ILI to rent out some portion of the 
building to the Government by the ILI. ILI has rented out 13184 Sq. Feet portion of the building 
to the Department of Legal Affairs. As per the recommendation of the committee, the 
Department of Legal Affairs may consider vacating the rented portion of the premises, for 
optimum utilization of the infrastructure of ILI, when the Central Vista made operational, 
accommodating all offices of the Department of Legal Affairs in the Central Vista. 
Further Observation  
3.6 The Indian Law Institute (ILI) was founded primarily with the objective of 
promoting and conducting legal research. After more than six decades of its coming into 
existence the institute is expected to  have evolved itself into a center of excellence in the 
field of Law. For this , the Government should provide adequate funds for running the 
institute and augmenting its infrastructure. On the other hand the ILI should generate 
more funds from research/consulting activ ities and gradually become self sufficient in 
terms of finances.

CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW OF THE DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND 
TRAINING 
Introduction 
1.0. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the nodal 
Ministry for matters relating to personnel management in the Government of India. 
1.1. The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T) 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) 
(iii) Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DPPW) 
 
 
1.2. The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Hon‘ble Prime 
Minister assisted by the Minister of State. The Department of Personnel and Training 
is functioning under the charge of a Secretary. 
1.3. Department of Personnel and Training formulates policies concerning 
recruitment, training, career progression, staff welfare and the post-retirement 
dispensation.  
Divisions of DoPT:  
1.4 Various wings of DoPT are as under: 
Ministry of 
Personnel Public 
Grievances and 
Pensions
Department of 
Personnel and 
Training
Department of 
Administrative 
Reforms and 
Public Grievances
Department of 
Pension and

Welfare

 
11 
(i) Establishment Officer's (EO) Wing - The Establishment Officer's Wing 
deals with the matters relating to senior appointments under the 
Government of India requiring approval of the Appointments 
Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). 
(ii) Services & Vigilance (S&V) Wing - The Services & Vigilance Wing 
handles matters relating to administration of Rules on all the service 
matters in respect of All India Services and acts as the nodal agency in 
the arena of vigilance and anti-corruption. This wing in addition to 
governing the implementation of RTI Act, also handles the 
administrative matters relating to the Administrative Tribunals and 
Central Information Commission. This wing also handles the work 
related to cadre restructuring in respect of the other Central Services. 
(iii) Establishment (Estt.) Wing - The Establishment Wing is responsible 
for framing and revising rules and regulations regarding service 
conditions of the employees and personnel policies of the Central 
Government employees other than All India Service Officers. This 
wing also handles the work related to Reservation Policy of the 
Government, Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) and Civil Services 
Officers' Institute (CSOI). 
(iv) Training (Trg.) Wing - The Training Wing acts as the nodal agency for 
training of Government functionaries and is primarily responsible for 
formulating policies with regard to training. 
(v) Administration Wing - Administration Wing deals with the matters 
related to cadre management of the Central Secretariat Service, 
Central Secretariat Stenographers Service and the Central Secretariat 
Clerical Service. This wing also handles the administrative matters 
relating to the State Re-organization, Reservation Policy of the 
Government and Welfare Activities for benefit of the employees of 
the Government except CSOI. 
Functions of DoPT: 
1.5. The following functions have been allocated to the Department of Personnel & 
Training as per the Business of Allocation Rules: 

 
12 
1. Recruitment for All India and Central Services through Civil Services 
Examination.  
2. Placement of successful candidates to various Services/Cadres; 
Officers under Central Staffing Scheme.  
3. Cadre Management of IAS and three Secretariat Services (Central 
Secretariat Service, Central Secretariat Stenographers' Service & 
Central Secretariat Clerical Service).  
4. Administrative vigilance - to oversee and provide necessary directions 
to the Government‘s programme of maintaining discipline and 
eradicating corruption from public services. 
5. Formulation and implementation of the policy related to Right to 
Information Act, 2005.  
6. Formulation and implementation of policy of reservation in services 
under the Government of India.  
7. Welfare of Central Government Employees. 
8. Administrative Tribunals.  
9. Increasing the efficiency of public services along with the well-being 
of the employees through Joint Consultative Machinery.  
10. Capacity Building/Training. 
11. Framing personnel policies in respect of various service matters 
applicable to the Central Government employees. 
Mandate of DoPT: 
1.6 The details of some of the functions performed by DoPT are as follows: 
Senior Appointments under the Government of India 
1.7 The Department of Personnel & Training (DoPT) looks after appointments at 
senior levels in the Government. For this purpose, the Establi shment Officer in the 
Department is the Secretary to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC).  
All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India requiring 
approval of the ACC, as per the Government of India (Transaction of Busines s Rules) 
1961 are processed through the Establishment Officer. These include Board level 
appointments in Public Sector Undertakings and appointment to posts at the level of 
Joint Secretary. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require approval of 
the ACC, are also processed through the Establishment Officer.  
1.8 The Establishment Officer is the Member Secretary of the Civil Services 
Board (CSB) chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. The Establishment Officer also assists 

 
13 
the Screening Committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary for considering cases of 
Foreign Assignments for All India Service (AIS) officers and members of the 
organized Group A and Group B Services of the Central Government (Officers of JS 
level & above). 
The Central Staffing Scheme 
1.9 The Central Staffing Scheme provides a systematic arrangement for the 
selection and appointment of officers to senior administrative posts at the Centre, 
excluding posts which are specifically encadred for the organized Group 'A' services 
or filled by recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, by borrowing 
from the All India Services and participating Group 'A' services. The raison d‘être of 
such a scheme is the Centre's need for fresh inputs at senior levels in policy 
formulation and programme implementation from diverse sources viz. the All -India 
Services and the participating organized Group 'A' Services. The officers serve for 
specified periods on deputation and return to their respective cadres at the end of their 
tenure. This two -way movement is of mutual benefit to the service cadres and the 
Government of India. 
Central Deputation Reserve 
1.10 The Establishment Officers (EO) Division in the Department of Personnel & 
Training maintains an electronic database of the IAS off icers & of Group ‗A‘ service 
officers working at the Centre under the Central Staffing Scheme. These records are 
maintained on the basis of orders/letters/notifications issued by the DoPT, various 
Central Ministries/Departments and the State Governments.  The maintenance/ 
updation of this database is significant, as it helps in providing readily available 
digitized information in respect of all officers and also processing of cases for foreign 
appointments/assignments and training etc.  
Cadre Management 
1.11 The Services Division of DoPT is responsible for Cadre Management of All 
India Services (IAS, IPS and IFS) which includes framing and revising rules and 
regulations regarding service conditions of the employees, in consultation with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of Environment and Forests. Matters relating 
to framing and amendment of recruitment rules, clarification related to rules etc., are 
examined and processed in this Division. 
 
 
 

 
14 
Anti Corruption 
1.12 The Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal D epartment for anti -
corruption. This Division acts in conjunction with specialized agencies like the 
Central Vigilance Commission, Central Bureau of Investigation, Enforcement 
Directorate and other line Ministries entrusted with the s pecific tasks within their 
respective administrative domain, viz. corporate governance, extradition matters, 
prevention of money laundering, mutual legal assistance treaties etc. 
1.13 India is also a Member of G-20 Anti-Corruption Working Group. The focus of 
this Group is towards the global financial system, particularly from the point of view 
of denial of entry or visa to corrupt officials, providing measures to protect whistle 
blowers, promote effective functioning of anti -corruption bodies and associatio n of 
private and business sector in combating corruption. India has been participating in 
Anti-Corruption Working Group (ACWG) meetings.  
Reservation in the Central Government Service 
1.14 DoPT issues instructions on the matters regarding reservation in posts and 
services in Central Government for the following:- 
(i) Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes & Other Backward Classes; 
(ii) Economically Weaker Sections who are not covered under the scheme 
 of reservation for SCs, STs and OBCs; 
(iii) Persons with Benchmark Disabilities; 
(iv) Ex-servicemen 
Joint Consultative Machinery 
1.15 A well-structured three-tier machinery is in place for joint consultation 
between the Central Government and its employees for promoting harmonious 
relations and securing the greatest measure of cooperation between the Central 
Government and the general body of employees in matters of common concern. The 
objective is to increase the efficiency of public services along with the well-being of 
the employees. The three tiers of Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) are: 
(i) National Council- at the apex level, functioning under the Department of 
Personnel and Training; 
(ii) Department Councils- functioning at Ministries/ Departments level; and 
(iii) Office Councils- functioning at offices/organizations under various 
Ministries/ Departments. 

 
15 
Service matters having a bearing on the administration and the general interests of the 
Government employees are dealt with by this machinery. 
National Anomaly Committee   
1.16 The National Anomaly Committee has been set up under the Chairm anship of 
Secretary (Personnel)  to settle the anomalies arising out of the implementation of 
recommendation the Seventh Central Pay Commission‘s recommendations.  
Training 
1.17 The Training Division of the Department of Personnel and Training is the 
nodal agency for training of government functionaries and is primarily responsible for 
formulating policies concerning training. It also implements certain components of 
training directly. In the implementation of its mandate, the Division has set the 
following objectives: 
 Administering Policy matters in training 
 Identification of functional areas of training 
 Designing and implementing training programs for officers involved in 
the priority development sectors 
 Development of trainers and training capability 
Right to Information  
1.18 The IR Division of DoPT is mandated to perform the following functions: 
 Administration of the RTI Act and Rules including amendm ents 
thereof. 
 Issue of Guidelines and clarification on RTI. 
 Implementation of the Annual Programme titled ‗Improving 
Transparency and Accountability in Government through Effective 
Implementation of RTI Act‘. 
 Management of RTI online web portal. 
 Administrative matters of Central Information Commission. 
 Appointment of Chief Information Commissioner and Information 
Commissioners in the Central Information Commission.  
 Framing of the Law regarding the Right to Privacy 
Welfare  
1.19. Realising that improvement in the working and living conditions of the 
employees and their families leads to efficiency and high morale, the Department 
supports various welfare programmes. These are provided through Recreation Halls/ 

 
16 
Clubs in various Ministries/ De partments, Central Government Employees Welfare 
Coordination Committees in Central Government Offices located outside Delhi, 
Residents‘ Welfare Association /Area Welfare Officers, Benevolent Fund and 
Departmental canteens.  
1.20 Department of Personnel and  Training is the nodal agency for four registered 
societies set up for the welfare of Government employees and their families. These 
societies are the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan 
Kendra, Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board and Kendriya Bhandar.  
Mission Karmayogi 
1.21 Civil services are at the centre of all government activities — they are agents 
of Policy making and the executive hand that delivers on the ground. The skill  sets 
and capacity of the civil servants play a vital role in service delivery, program 
implementation and performing core governance functions. Recognising this crucial 
responsibility, the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building 
(NPCSCB) aims to create a professional, well -trained and future-looking civil service 
that is imbued with a shared understanding of India's developmental aspirations, 
national programs and priorities. The focus of NPCSCB is on promoting ease of 
living and ease of doing business, by considerably enhancing the ci tizen-government 
interface. This involves creation of both functional and behavioural competencies 
among the civil servants. 
e-HRMS 
1.22 To facilitate digital working environment in Central Government, an 
electronic Human Resources Management System (e -HRMS) has been introduced in 
all the Departments. This will help Government to digitally manage the service 
matters of officials leading to reduction in transaction time and cost, availability of 
digital records, dashboards for MIS, real time monitoring of manpower deployment as 
well as serving as a productivity enhancement tool amongst others. The e -HRMS will 
be integrated with the i-GOT-Karmayogi platform. 
Bodies under the administrative control of DoPT: 
1.23 The Department of Personnel and Training also han dles the administrative 
work relating to the following Institutions: -  
(i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) 
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 

 
17 
(iii) Lokpal 
(iv) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) 
(v) Central Information Commission (CIC)

(ix) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) 
(x) Capacity Building Commission  
(xi) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) 
(xii) Institute of Secretariat Training & Management (ISTM) 
(xiii) Special Purpose Vehicle –Karmayogi Bharat  
Union Public Service Commission 
1.24 UPSC is a Constitutional Body mandated to discharge the  duties, functions 
and obligations assigned under Article 320. It conducts various examinations  in 
accordance with the Rules of examination as notified by the Government of India in a 
just, fair and impartial manner  for making a merit based selection and 
recommendation of candidates for various Group A and Group B Services of the 
Govt. of India. 
Central Vigilance Commission 
1.25 Central Vigilance Commission was initially set up through Re solution of 
Government of India  on the recommendations of Committee on Prevention of 
Corruption formed under the Chairmanship of Shri K. Santhanam.  It was accorded 
statutory status in 2003.  Central Vigilance Commission consists of a Central 
Vigilance Commissioner as Chairperson and not more than two Vigilance 
Commissioners as Members.   
Lokpal 
1.26 Lokpal is a statutory body constituted under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act,  
2013. It has jurisdiction to inquire into allegations of corruption against anyone who is 
or has been Prime Minister, or a Minister in the Union government, or a Member of 
Parliament, as well as officials of the Union Government under Groups A, B, C and 
D. Also covered are chairpersons,  members, officers and directors of any board, 
corporation, society, trust or autonomous body either established by an Act of 

 
18 
Parliament or wholly or partly funded by the Union or State government. It also 
covers any society or trust or body that receives foreign contribution above ₹10 lakh. 
Central Administrative Tribunal 
1.27 Although there are elaborate rules and regulations for Personnel Management, 
there are Government employees who feel aggrieved by the Government decisions. 
The Courts used to take many years to decide these cases and litigation was 
expensive. In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved 
by Government decisions, the Government set up the Central Administrative Tribunal 
(CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases relating to service matters which were 
previously dealt with by courts upto and including the High Court. There are 19  
Benches and 19 Circuit Benches in the Central Administrative Tribunal all over India. 
The Government of India has notified 215 organizations including Ministries and 
Departments of Central Government, under section 14 (2) of the Administrative 
Tribunals A ct, 1985 to bring them within the jurisdiction of the Central 
Administrative Tribunal, from time to time. In addition the Central Administrative 
Tribunal, Principal Bench is dealing with the matters of Govt. of National Capital 
Territory of Delhi. 
Central Information Commission 
1.28 Central Information Commission is a statutory body constituted under the 
Right to Information Act, 2005. The jurisdiction of the Commission extends over all 
Central Public Authorities. The Commission has certain powers and functions such as 
adjudication in  second appeal for giving information; direction for record keeping, 
suo motu disclosures receiving and enquiring into a  complaint on inability to file RTI 
etc; imposition of penalties and Monitoring and Reporting including preparation of an 
Annual Report. The decisions of the Commission are final and binding. 
Central Bureau of Investigation 
1.29 CBI is the premier investigating agency in India.  Cases are referred to this 
agency, on the basis of concurrence of the State Governments, by the High Court as 
well as by the Supreme Court.  It is also the nodal agency which coordinates 
investigation on behalf of Interpol Member Countries. 
Staff Selection Commission 
1.30 SSC is one of the largest recruiting agencies of the Government of India. The 
Commission is mandated with the task of making recruitment to all Group B (Non 
Gazetted) and Group C (Non Technical)  posts in various Ministries/Departments of 

 
19 
the Government of India and their Attached and Subordinate offices except those 
posts which are specifically exempted from the purview of the Commission. In 
addition, the Commission, from the year 2016, has been assigned the additional 
responsibility of making recruitments to Group B (Gazetted) posts of Assistant 
Accounts officer and Assistant Audit officer for the Indian Audit and Accounts 
Department. Further, in the year 2021, the Staff Selection Commission has been 
entrusted with the responsibility of conducting recruitment examinations for the 
vacant Group B (Non Gazetted) and Group C posts in Constitutional/Statutory bodies 
and the Union Territory of Ladakh. 
National Recruitment Agency  
1.31 NRA is an autonomo us body mandated to conduct a Common Eligibility Test 
(CET) to shortlist candidates for vacancies of Group ‗B‘ Non Gazetted Posts, Group 
B Gazetted Posts, which are exempted from consultation with UPSC, Group C posts 
in the Government and equivalent posts (Where no such classification exists).CET 
shall be a computer based Online Tier I examination. 
Public Enterprises Selection Board 
1.32 Public Enterprises Selection Board is a high powered body set up with the 
objective of evolving a sound managerial policy  for the Central Public Sector 
Enterprises and, in particular, to advise Government on appointments to their top 
management posts. It consists of a Chairperson and three Members. 
Capacity Building Commission 
1.33 Capacity Building Commission has been manda ted to drive standardisation 
and harmonisation across the Indian civil services landscape. As the custodian of civil 
services capacity building reforms, the Commission‘s role is central to the overall 
institutional framework of Mission Karmayogi.  Established as an independent body 
with complete executive and financial autonomy, the Commission comprises of three 
Members and is supported by an internal Secretariat.  CBC is mandated to perform 
the following key functions: 
 Preparing an Annual State of Civil Services Report 
 Exercising functional supervision over Training Institutions and creating 
shared learning resources 
 Facilitating the creation of Annual Capacity Building Plans for ministries 
and departments 
 Organising a global HR Summit 

 
20 
 Evolving a harmonious,  de-siloed approach to capacity building 
initiatives 
 Undertaking Audit of Human Resources available in Government 
 Recommending policy interventions in areas of personnel/HR to DoPT 
 Approving Knowledge Partners for the Mission 
Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA) 
1.34 The Lal Bahadur Shastri Nati onal Academy of Administration, located in 
Mussoorie, is India's premier research and training institute on administration and 
public policy. LBSNAA conducts various training modules for civil servants posted at 
different ranks. A Foundation Course is held for the young entrants to the All India 
Services and other central Services. This is followed by a professional training of 
recruits to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) i ncluding members of the Royal 
Bhutan Administrative Service. The Academy also conducts the Mid -Career Training 
Program (MCTP) for members of the IAS and an Induction Training Program for 
officers promoted to the IAS from the state civil services.. 
Institute of Secretariat Training & Management (ISTM) 
1.35 Established in 1948 as Secretariat Training School, ISTM is mandated to 
conduct training programmes of Central Secretariat Service (CSS) and Central 
Secretariat Stenographers Service (CSSS) and other Organized services of the Central 
Secretariat. The Institute also imparts training to the officers of the Central and State 
Governments. Public sector undertakings, Autonomous bodies and the Union 
Territory Administrations. 
Special Purpose Vehicle –Karmayogi Bharat  
1.36 Karmayogi Bharat is a not-for-profit company, under the administrative 
control of DoPT, incorporated  as a 100% government owned entity for owning, 
managing, maintaining and  improving the digital assets, i.e.,  i-GOT-Karmayogi - the 
digital learning platform, on behalf of Government as part of the overall National 
Programme for  Civil Services Capacity Building. The SPV will have the 
responsibility to create  and operationalize the content marketplace and continuously 
evaluate its utilization.

in the processing of cases. Central Vigilance Commission may, accordingly, seek

3.2 DoPT informed the Committee that a Committee had been constituted under 
the Chairmanship of Shri C.Chandramouli  (former Secretary, DoPT) for making 
recommendations on various aspects concerning the IAS Cadre Strength including the 
determination of intake of Direct recruit IAS officers every year through Civil 
Services Examination from CSE 2022 to CSE 2030. The Comm ittee has submitted its 
report to DoPT and the same is under consideration. 
3.3 The Committee notes that there is a huge shortage of 1472 IAS officers in 
the country. The Committee infers from the data provided by DoPT that there 
are 850 vacancies in the D irect recruitment posts and 622 vacancies in the 
promotion posts. The Committee notes that in order to address the issue of 
shortage of IAS officers and to ensure their optimal intake, Central Government 
has been recruiting 180 IAS officers on annual basis  through Civil Services 
Examination.  The Committee recommends DoPT to consider increasing the 
annual intake of Direct recruit IAS officers further to bridge the deficit. The 
Committee further notes that the deficit of IAS officers stems partly from the 
fact that promotion quota IAS vacancies are not being filled up by states on time. 

 
45 
This issue needs to be taken up by the Centre with the State Governments and 
the Centre should impress u pon them to take immediate steps to fill up 
promotion quota IAS vacanci es on time so that shortage of IAS officers at the 
state level can be meted out which will help in effective functioning of the 
Government.  
3.4 On being asked about the impact of IAS crunch on administration, DoPT  
stated that the total authorized strength comprises Senior Duty Posts and 
various reserves such as State Deputation Reserve, Junior Reserve, Leave 
Reserve, Training Reserve and Central Deputation Reserve. Of these reserves, 
except for the Central Deputation reserve, all other reserves are being utilized by 
the States. DoPT further said that out of the prescribed Central Deputation 
Reserve of 1469, only 442 officers are working at the centre. The Committee is of 
the considered opinion that IAS officers are a common and shared asset of the 
country and therefore, it is incumbent upon them to serve both the Centre and 
States.

3.9 The Committee  notes that a large number of IAS officers are not filing 
Annual Immovable Property Returns. The Committee  also notes that India is a 
signatory to the United Nations Convention against Corruption  which mandates 
the state parties to establish and promote ef fective practices aimed at the 
prevention of corruption . The Committee further notes that DoPT is the nodal 
Department for anti -corruption including the matters concerning UNCAC.  
Keeping the wider ramifications of corruption in public administration in min d, 
the Committee recommends the Central Government to constitute a Committee 
to examine the issue of Non -submission of Annual Immovable Property Returns 
by public servants in detail. The Committee also feels that DoPT should put a 
mechanism in place to che ck the veracity of the property return statement filed 
by public servants. 
Menstrual Leave  
3.10  On being asked whether DoPT  is considering introducing menstrual leave for 
the benefit of women employees of the Central Government, the Department stated 
that there is no such proposal under consideration. 
3.11 The Committee notes that menstruation debilitates most women and 
affects their productivity and performance at workplace.  The Committee notes 
that, at present, there is no policy in place to address this need. The Committee 
takes note of Article 42 of the Indian Constitution which directs the state to make 
provision for  securing ‘just and humane’ conditions of work. The Committee 
further takes note of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social 
and Cultural Rights  which recognizes the right of everyone to  ‘just and 

 
48 
favourable’ working conditions . The Comm ittee is of the view that the 
Government should create an inclusive and equitable work place for women. 
Keeping the physical and mental well being of women in mind and taking 
cognizance of their unique needs, the Committee, recommends the  Department 
to ho ld consultations with stakeholders and  frame a menstrual leave policy 
allowing women who suffer from menstrual cramps, dysmenorrhea and similar 
conditions to take time off from their work.   The Government may consider 
granting a certain number of ‘Menstrual leaves’ or ‘sick leaves/Half Pay Leaves’ 
per month /year for women without seeking any medical certificate or 
justification in return. The Committee feels that this measure will have a positive 
impact on the female labour force participation rate in the formal sector and will 
help unlock the gender dividend for inclusive and broad-based growth.  
Personnel Policies  
3.12 Keeping in view the utmost importance attached to the enhancement of 
women‘s status in all walks of life and to enable them to lead a normal family life and 
also to ensure the education and welfare of children, DoPT issued guidelines for 
posting husband and wife who are in Government service at the same station. 
3.13 Point (ii) of the guidelines reads as under: 
 ‗Where one spouse belongs to one of the All India Services and the other 
spouse belongs to one of the Central Services - The Cadre Controlling authority of the 
Central Service may post the officer to the station or if there is no post in that station, 
to the state where the spouse belonging to the All India Service is posted‘.  
3.14 The guidelines further provide that complaints are sometimes received  that 
even if posts are available in the station of posting of the spouse, the administrative 
authorities do not accommodate the employees citing administrative reasons. In all 
such cases, the Cadre Controlling authority should strive to post the employee at the 
station of the spouse and in case of inability to do so, specific reasons therefor, may 
be communicated to the employee. 
3.15 The Committee appreciates the Department of Personnel and Training 
for formulating guidelines for posting husband and wife who are in Government 
service at the same station.  However, the Committee feels that there is a lacuna 
in the policy which needs to be addressed. It is observed that DoPT’s guidelines 
do not provide any relief to spouses where one of the spouses belongs to  an All 
India Service and the other spouse belongs to the Indian Foreign Service. The 
IFS does not have positions earmarked in the state Governments except for 

 
49 
postings in Regional Passport Offices and Branch Secretariats. Moreover, these 
positions are restricted to certain pay levels. Secondly, the AIS officer can opt for 
deputation but the rules require him /her to go back to the cadre for ‘cooling off’ 
period or in case of other exigencies.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends 
that appropriate guidelines  to extend the relief envisioned in t he above 
mentioned guidelines be framed for AIS-IFS couple also.  The Department may 
further consider allocating the AIS officer to AGMUT cadre and post him/her in 
Delhi or alternatively allocate him/her to the States co ntiguous to Delhi where 
the IFS officer remains posted for long periods  to the extent possible so that the 
couple can remain posted at the same station.

A.  Union Public Service Commission 
4.1 Union Public Service Commission comprises a Chairman and ten Members. It 
makes recruitment for All India Services, Group ‗A‘ Central Civil Services/posts, and 
Group ‗B‘ Gazetted posts in Ministries/Departments of the Central Government. The 
Commission also conducts examination for recruitment of Commissioned officers in 
the Defence forces. Some Union Territories (UTs) also avail the services of the Union 
Public Service Commission for recruitment to the posts under the UT.   
4.2 The functions of the Commissi on are as specified in Article 320 of the 
Constitution. By the exercise of powers conferred by the proviso to Article 320 (3) of 
the Constitution , the President has made the UPSC (Exemption from Consultation) 
Regulations, 1958 as amended from time to time,  as respects the All India Services 
and also as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the 
Union specifying the matters in which it shall not be necessary for the UPSC to be 
consulted.

4.4 The Committee notes from the data provided by UPSC that the average  
time taken for civil services examination from the date of issue of Notification to 

 
51 
the date of declaration of final result is nearly 15 months.  The Committee is of 
the opinion that the duration of any recruitment examination should not  
ordinarily exceed six m onths as long and protracted recruitment cycles waste 
prime years of a candidates’ life besides taking a heavy toll on their physical and 
mental health. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that UPSC should take 
steps to reduce the duration of the recruitment cycle significantly without 
compromising the quality. 
4.5 UPSC apprised the Committee that it releases the answer key of the 
preliminary test of the Civil services examination only after the completion of the 
entire process of the said examination.  In other words, the Commission is 
depriving the candidates of an opportunity to contest the answer key before 
progressing to the next stage of the said examination.  This practice not only 
demoralizes the candidates but also compromises the validity and fairness of the 
examination process. Although recruiting agencies exercise utmost caution to 
ensure that the answer key is fool proof, the possibility of errors cannot be ruled 
out. The Committee, therefore, recommends that UPSC may  take steps to 
publish the answer key right after the preliminary stage of the civil services 
examination and allow candidates to raise objections. The Committee further 
recommends that UPSC may also collect feedback from the candidates and effect 
improvements in the examination system from time to time  to ensure more 
transparency, fairness and candidate friendliness. 
Impact Assessment  
4.6 The Committee had  recommended in its previous Reports that an expert 
committee should be constituted to study the impa ct of the changes carried out in the 
scheme and syllabus of Civil Services Examination from time to time on 
administration and candidates.  
4.7 On being asked about the progres s made in this regard, UPSC informed the 
Committee that it had requested DoPT to take a decision first on the recommendations 
of the Baswan Committee, and thereafter, approach the Commission to constitute 
another Expert Committee, if the situation so warrants. 
4.8 The Committee has  recommended in its 104 th, 106 th, 108 th and 112 th 
Reports that an expert Committee must be constituted to assess the impact of the 
changes brought about by the Commission in the scheme of Civil Services 
examination since 2010 on administration and candidates.  UPSC has time and 
again reiterated  that the r eport of Baswan Committee is under consideration . 

 
52 
The Committee is aware that Baswan Committee was constituted to make 
recommendations on the eligibility, Syllabus, Scheme and Pattern of 
Examination. However, w hat the Committee has been emphatic about in i ts 
recommendations is ‘Administrative Impact Assessment’, i.e. an assessment of 
the impact of administrative decisions. While UPSC has changed the pattern of 
Civil Services Examination from time to time on the basis of recommendations 
made by various Exper t Committees, no study has been commissioned to assess 
how such changes impacted the aspirants, nature of recruitment and 
administration at large. The Committee reiterates its recommendation that an 
expert group or Committee should be appointed to assess the impact of  changes 
made in the scheme, pattern and syllabus of Civil services examination in the last 
ten years on the quality of recruitment and administration at large. The expert 
group so constituted may assess if the present scheme of recruitment pro vides an 
equal opportunity to both English -medium educated urban candidates and non -
english medium educated rural candidates. The expert group may also assess 
whether the existing pattern of preliminary and mains examination provides a 
level playing field for all candidates irrespective of their academic background.  
The Committee is of the considered opinion that DoPT /UPSC should consider 
making further changes in the scheme and syllabus of Civil Services 
Examination in the light of the findings of the Impact Assessment study. 
 
B.      Staff Selection Commission 
 
4.9 Staff Selection Commission is one of the largest recruiting agencies in India in 
terms of number of candidates who apply for various posts in the Central 
Government. It  is mandated to make recruitment to Group ‗B‘ (Non -Gazetted) and 
Group ‗C‘ (Non -Technical) Posts in the Government of India. The Commission has 
also been assigned the responsibility of recruitment to Group ‗B‘ (Gazetted) Posts of 
Assistant Accounts Officer and Assistant Audit Officer for the Indian Audit and 
Accounts Department. 
4.10 The Committee appreciates  Staff Selection Commission for making 
efforts to squeeze the recruitment cycle  to 6 -9 months.  The Commission 
informed the Committee that it has decided to do away with the descriptive 
examinations in an attempt to expedite the recruitment cycle. The Committee is 
of the considered opinion that the skills of the personnel should be in consonance 

 
53 
with their job requirements.  Candidates requiring to take up high management 
posts are required to have aptitude, in -depth knowledge, good writing skills and 
communication abilities . Therefore, the Committee recommends SSC to 
reconsider its decision to do away with the descriptive tests. 
4.11 The Committee takes cognizance of the manpower constraints being faced 
by the Commission in th e wake of transition to online mode of conduct of 
examinations and accordingly recommends DoPT to provide specialized 
personnel and adequate infrastructure to the meet the requirements of the 
Commission.  
C. National Recruitment Agency 
4.12  National Recruitment Agency (NRA) has been set up  as an autonomous body 
to conduct a Common Eligibility Test (CET) to shortlist candidates for vacancies of 
Group 'B' Non -Gazetted posts, Group 'B' Gazetted posts, which are exempted from 
consultation with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC); Group ‗C‘ posts in 
the Government and equivalent posts (where no such classifications exist) thro ugh a 
computer-based Tier-I examination.  
4.13  To begin with, NRA will conduct a separate CET for the three levels viz., 
graduate, higher secondary (12th pass) and the matriculate (10th pass) candidates for 
those non -technical posts to which recruitment i s carried out by the Staff Selection 
Commission (SSC), the Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) and by the Institute of 
Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS).  
4.14 The score obtained by candidates in CET will be shared with the SSC, RRB & 
IBPS for their next le vel (Tier -II onwards) examinations for selection to various 
Government jobs. The score, obtained by the candidate in the CET, will be valid for 
three years and the highest score obtained in the last three years shall be taken as the 
score for consideration  in the next level of recruitment process by the respective 
recruitment bodies. Therefore, the candidate can appear in multiple Tier -II and 
onward examinations as long as score is valid and the candidate is shortlisted by those 
recruitment bodies. 
4.15 NRA has been registered as a Society under the Societies Reg istration Act, 
1860 with its Head Office in Delhi NCR. NRA has a Governing Body at the Apex 
Level to give strategic direction to  it. The composition of the Governing Body is as 
follows:

4.16 The Chairman of National Recruitment Agency informed the Committee 
that NRA is undertaking a detailed study of examination practices so that the 
problems encountered by other recruitment agencies are addressed ab initio. The 
Committee recommends NRA to hold consultations with stakeholders and weigh 
the pros and cons of existing system of multiple examinations and the proposed 
system of single examination and evolve a model that strikes a harmonious 
balance between the two.  The Committee hopes that these fundamental issues 
are addressed at the earliest and the f irst common eligibility Test would be held 
soon. 
4.17  Keeping in view the difficulties encountered by candidates especially  
differently abled and women candidates, the Committee recommends Union 
Public Service Commission, Staff Selection Commission and National 
Recruitment agencies to take steps to ensure that candidates are allotted an 
examination centre within 5 kilometres from their home as far as practicable.
