Special Campaign on Swachta and reducing pendency in Government offices: 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.47 The Committee applauds the Department in bringing out such innovative ideas  for 
cleanliness campaign. The Committee hopes that the Department will hold such  campaigns 
every year. The Committee expects the Department to widen  the scope of such campaigns so 
that more number of offices can be included in the campaign. (3.25) 
Action Taken  
1.48 From 2021, the Government of India has started a month -long Special Campaign 
from 2nd -31st October every year on the Disposal of Pending Matters (SCDPM) and 
institutionalizing Swachhata at work place in all Central Ministries/Departments including 
their attached/subordinate offices.  Two Special Campaigns have been conducted so far in the 
year 2021 and 2022. 
1.49 The Special campaign in the year 2021, organized from 2nd —31st October, 2021 
focussed on Ministries/ Departments and had very encouraging outcome s. Swachhata 
camapigns were made at 5,968 sites.  About 12 lakh square feet of space was freed from 
scrap and outlived records and Rs 62.54 crore of revenue earned through disposal of scrap.  
1.50 The Special Campaign 2.0 was implemented in Central Governm ent from October 2 -
October 31, 2022 with the objective of institutionalizing swachhata and minimizing pendency 
in government. Under the Special Campaign 2.0, 5.6 lac public grievances were redressed, 
cleanliness campaign was carried out in 1.01 lac office spaces, 37.50 lac files were weeded 
out, 89.5 lakh square feet of space was freed, and scrap disposal earned Rs. 370.1 crores. The 
special campaign 2.0 brought in a number of success stories in digitization, efficient 
management of office spaces, enhanceme nt of office premises, environment friendly 
practices, inclusivity, protocols and mechanisms being put in place and waste disposal.  

 
 
 
 36 
1.51 Departments/ Ministries gave special attention to attached/ subordinate/ field offices 
including in the remotest parts  of India in the month long campaign. Special Campaign 2.0 
was 17 times larger than Special Campaign of 2021 in terms of cleanliness campaign sites.  
1.52 The Special Campaign 2.0 was perhaps the biggest Campaign of office reforms in 
terms of size and scal e. It has helped decluttering offices, better space management and 
cleaner work environment in addition to effective management of records.  In order to 
maintain thrust of the campaign throughout the year and institutionalizing swachhata and 
decision-making reforms, the portal ( https://www.pgportal.gov.in/SCDPM/) and institution of 
nodal officers in each Ministry has been continued.  Ministries are uploading information on 
this portal every month and DARPG br ings out monthly publication on Secretariat Reforms 
based on the data uploaded by the Ministries.  Report of the month of April 2023 is enclosed. 
1.53 The Special campaign has now become a permanent activity and during October, 
2023, Special campaign 3.0 i s proposed to be undertaken with further enlargement of scope.  
This year the campaign is proposed to cover Ministries/ Departments, attached/ subordinate/ 
field offices, PSUs in the Central Government.  A meeting with Secretaries of Administrative 
Reforms of all States/ UTs was also held on 31st May, 2023 wherein they also showed 
willingness to participate in the month long Special Campaign during the month of October, 
2023.   Therefore, the Special campaign 3.0 is expected to be a much larger campaign 
covering all Offices of Government of India as well as the State/ UT Governments.    
1.54 Further,  with a view to encourage and develop a healthy competition  amongst all 
Ministries/ Departments for various activities under the Special campaign, a category i s 
proposed to be introduced in this year‘s prime Minister‘s Award for performance of 
Ministries/ Departments under the Special campaign, for which details are being worked out. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.55 The Committee recommends the Department to enco urage and aid the States also to 
carry out such campaigns for cleaning of State Government offices and attached/subordinate 
officers under the State Government, in a time-bound manner. (3.26) 
Action Taken  
1.56 A meeting with Secretaries of Administrative Reforms of all States/ UTs was held on 
31st May, 2023 to discuss recommendations of 127th Report of Parliamentary Standing 

 
 
 
 37 
Committee for replication/ dissemination of best practices of Special Campaign for 
institutionalizing Swachhata and reducing pendency and other initiatives of Secretariat 
reforms of the Government.  All States/ UTs expressed their willingness to participate in 
Special Campaign on Reducing pendency and institutionalizing Swachhata.  It was dec ided 
that DARPG will help the States to structure the Campaign and develop online system of 
coordination and monitoring of the Campaign.   As the Campaign of such a scale requires 
massive outreach and mobilization, DARPG also agreed to support the States i n developing 
Communication strategy for the Special Campaign in 2023.  
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR GOOD GOVERNANCE (NCGG) 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.57 The Committee appreciates the  Capacity Building Programme  conducted by NCGG 
in collaboration with different countries and recommends signing MoU with  more and more 
countries as the success of these programmes enhance the image not only of the institution 
but also of the country and plays a vital role to strengthen the bilateral relations. (3.31) 
Action Taken  
1.58 India has created a niche for itself in providing citizen -centric governance,  
progressive public policies, faster socio -economic development, high economic growth and  
attainment of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) with speed and scale. This has 
improved the quality of life of citizens and world is talked about. Over the years, NCGG has 
been building its own capacity in these areas and has been able to create a name for itself on 
whom Ministry of External Affairs depends on developing and conducting need -based high 
quality capacity building programmes for the civil servants of developing countries and also 
giving advice to these governments. This brings a good name for the country and appreciated 
by the civil servants and government of various developing countries. 
1.59 NCGG designs and conducts comprehensive capacity building programmes for the 
civil servants of developing countries with the support of the Ministry of External Affairs. In 
2023-24, Ministry of External Affairs has substantially enhanced these programmes and 
approved45 capacity building programmes to impart training to 1,810 civil servants of 
Maldives, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Cambodia, Gambia, SriLanka, Mauritius, and other 
countries of Africa, LatinAmerica, etc. 

 
 
 
 38 
1.60 The modules for such programmes are developed in close collaboration with the 
concerned countries and Indian missions therein to meet their developmental needs. NCGG is 
in constant touch with the MEA for inclusion of more developing countries under the 
programme.The MEA has agreed in principle to include more countries in future and 
accordingly NCGG has planned to enhance and expand its own capacity in terms of human 
resources and domain expertise, and infrastructure facilities to include more developing 
countries in future programmes. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.61 The Committee aspires to see NCGG as a 'world class institute' in the field of  good 
governance. For that NCGG has developed a strategy which includes having its  own campus 
and office space, suitable infrastructure, and additional human resources to carryout 
diversified activities. The Committee hopes that NCGG will  implement such strategies and 
act as a premier thinktank of the Government of India. (3.32) 
Action Taken  
1.62 NCGG being an apex level institution is visited by high level dignitaries viz. High 
Commissioners/ Ambassadors and senior diplomats of various countries, eminent people,  
senior civil servants, domain experts, academicians, heads of various institutions of India and 
abroad, etc. As recommended by the Committee, NCGG has to have decent facilities to  
engage with such high ranking and eminent people and convey the right image of the country 
and of the institution. 
1.63 As suggested by the Committee that NCGG should also have its own independent 
campus to do its mandated work more effectively and efficiently. The matter was discussed 
with the DARPG and Ministry of Finance. During the discussion, it was fully supported and 
indicated that once land and its cost, building, and infrastructure is firmed up, the proposal for 
capital cost will be considered in a holistic manner. In the meantime, NCGG can take office 
space on rent as building its own campus, will take time and it needs dignified office space on 
urgent basis. Accordingly, Ministry of Finance has provided funds in RE (2022-23) as well as 
in 2023-24totaketheofficespace on rent and develop commensurate facilities. 
1.64 In short-term, NCGG is focusing on improving its existing facilities at Mussoorie as 
well as taking a proper office space on rent for its head office in Delhi. It plans to have 
meeting room, conference hall, e -governance facilities, classrooms, etc. to conduct training 
programmes, meetings, conferences, seminars, round table discussions, webinars, and 
executive hostel for resource persons, etc. 

 
 
 
 39 
1.65  As recommended by the Committee, NCGG is also working with the DARPG to 
create essential posts and fill the same on urgent basis to meet the additional human resources 
requirement so that diversified and expanded activities of NCGG are carried out effectively  
and efficiently. NCGG is also working on the strategy to bring various domain experts and  
eminent people on its roll so that quality output commensurate to its apex-level institution is 
given.

1.68 The chart clearly depicts the allocated amount and utilization pattern for such a very 
vital scheme of the Department. During 2021 -22 the BE allocation was Rs. 5 crores for the

CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
1.0 eCourts Mission Mode Project is an important Scheme of the Department 
aimed at improving access to justice using technology. The Government has released 
a total of Rs.935 crores and Rs.1670 crores under Phase -I and Phase -II of the 
Scheme, respectively. The Committee is appreciative of the fact that Phase -II of the 
project has performed exceedingly well. But the Committee in its visits to many of 
the High Courts in the country have found that after the waning of the pandemic 
many of the Judges are not c omfortable working with the virtual/hybrid courts and 
are back to old mode of physical hearings. Thus there is a real danger of 
infrastructure created under this project on the hard -earned public money being 
wasted. Accordingly, the Committee recommends th e Government to approach the 
eCommittee of the Supreme Court and to request them to issue guidelines for making 
full use of e -resources created for virtual/hybrid hearings in the courts, which is not 
only time saving but also economical.           (Para 1.34) 
 
Action Taken 
1.1   As recommended by the Hon‟ble Committee, the matter has already been 
addressed to eCommittee, Supreme Court of India. 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
1.2   Designing Innovative Solutions for Holistic Access to Justice in India 
(DISHA):- 
 
1.2(a)  The Committee appreciates the initiatives of the Department under the 
DISHA Scheme which seeks to prioritize citizen -centric justice delivery system by 
integrating access to justice with technology. The four components of the Scheme 
have been curated with the objective of strengthening pre-litigation mechanism (Tele-
Law); developing effective dispensation of pro -bono legal services (Nyaya Bandhu); 
facilitating disposal of pending cases in the courts through a cadre of retired Judges 
(Nyaya Mitra);and empowering citizens through PAN India legal literacy and legal 
awareness.                    (Para 1.38)

that apart from their ongoing efforts, they should make full use  of social media 
platforms like YouTube, Face book, Twitter, etc. through supply of quality content

reach, even to the grassroots and are affordable to the citizens. The De partment may 
use animations, talks by experts, etc. by way of making short videos, for educating 
the common public on their rights and also to generate awareness about the 
schemes/programmes of the Department.          (Para 1.39)

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF 
THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION 
2.0 The State is duty bound to provide easy access to Justice and timely delivery of 
Justice to all its citizen. Adequacy of judicial in frastructure plays a critical role in 
reduction of pendency and backlog of cases in the Courts. But it is an undeniable fact 
that the state of judicial infrastructure in the country is far from being satisfactory. 
Courts are functioning in rented premises with insufficient space and many in a 
dilapidated condition without basic amenities like toilets etc. In such a scenario, the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for 
Judiciary is playing a pivotal role in the devel opment of critical infrastructure at the 
State level.                       (Para 1.18) 
 
2.1  From the data provided by the Department of Justice, it can be seen that many 
of the States are utilizing this scheme in the best possible manner and have created 
substantial judicial infrastructure in their States. However, in many of the States 
nothing notable has happened under this Scheme.                     (Para 1.19) 
 
2.2    The Committee observes that the pace of release of funds has slowed down due 
to revised procedural guidelines for release of CSS funds under the new Public 
Financial Management System (PFMS). Due to stringent conditions attached for 
release of funds, most of the States are finding it difficult to get their quota of funds 
despite having huge requirements for funds for their projects both ongoing and new. 
From the data provided by the Department, 11 out of 21 general category States and 5 
out of 8 NE States did not get any funds during 2022 -23 due to such norms. Though 
the Committee is happy to note that the Department of Justice is taking all possible 
measures to ameliorate the har dship  faced by the States in this regard, and to ensure 
that all of them become PFMS compliant, the Committee, however, recommends the 
Department to approach the MoF to get the guidelines on release of funds under the 
CSS relaxed, wherever the States are facing genuine difficulties in the 
implementation of such guidelines.               (Para 1.20) 
2.3  The Committee in January, 2023 visited Assam, Manipur and Tripura to assess 
the judicial infrastructure and to have an on the spot assessment of implementation of 
this Scheme in the North Eastern Region. After deliberating with the concerned State 

 14 
Governments and High Court Judges on this issue, the Committee is constrained to 
note that the status of judicial infrastructure is in very bad shape in the region and 
they are not being able to make full use of this Scheme.         (Para 1.21) 
 
2.4   Apart from general PFMS related issues being faced by all the States/UTs, the 
North-Eastern States have their own issues because of their peculiar topography 
which makes availability of unencumbered land a bit difficult. Also the NE States 
and other hilly States are bestowed with short working season which makes 
movement of men and material difficult over the treacherous terrain and thereby 
making contract implementa tion difficult with increased time and cost overruns. 
Because of limited railways connectivity in the region, the cost of transportation 
becomes much higher, leading to substantial increase in cost of material. Other 
reasons include late receipt of project  proposals and non -receipt of utilization of 
certificates from the respective state governments. It has also been found that in case 
of North-eastern States, their contribution to the scheme though meagre (only 10% 
vis-à-vis 90% of Central share) gets dela yed. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends the Department to explore the possibility of providing a better deal in 
terms of enhanced allocation of funds and relaxation of spending norms under the 
Scheme, considering the peculiarities of the NE States. It is further recommended that 
the 10% of the state quota may also be relaxed for the NE States subject to 
subsequent recovery from the concerned state, so that the ongoing projects are not 
stalled for want of such meagre amount of money.          (Para 1.22) 
 
Action Taken 
2.5  As regards relaxation of PFMS guidelines, on earlier occasions, the 
matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance (MoF). However, MoF has made it 
categorically clear that all the States have to become PFMS compliant, as this is a 
reform measure to avoid parking of funds by the states  and also to ensure utilization 
of the funds meant for a scheme, in that scheme only.  After facing initial technical 
problems/hitches, all the States have since on -boarded the Public Financial 
Management System (PFMS) and are making expenditure through PFMS only. 
  
 As regards enhanced allocation to the NER States, as per the laid down norms, 
at least 10% of budget is to be utilized for NER states. Against provision of Rs.89.99 
crore for NER States (within total RE of Rs.848.00 Crore for the entire country 
under CSS for Development of Judicial Infrastructure ), during FY 2022 -23 against 
allocation of Rs.89.99 crore for NER, funds to the tune of Rs.122.50 crore have been 

 15 
released to NER states. Thus, subject t o availability of funds, the Department keeps 
on making efforts to provide enhanced allocation to the NER. The States have 
however, have the flexibility to prepare their design and Schedule of Rates (SOR) 
based on their local requirement and need. Further in the NER region there are 730 
Court Halls and 627 Residential Units of Judges/Judicial Officer covering District 
and Subordinate Courts, are available as on 30 th June, 2023. Moreover, 194 Court 
Halls and 148 Residential Units are under construction.  
  
 Further, as per the guidelines of Ministry of Finance, based on the funding 
pattern being followed in all the Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) being 
implemented by the Government, for the above CSS also, Central Share of funds is 
released in prescribed ra tio to all the States/UTs which is 60:40 (Centre : States), 
except 8 NER States and 2 Himalayan States (Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh) 
where the ratio is 90:10 and in UTs it is 100% Central funding. It is owing to the 
difficult terrain of NER States and  other hilly States that the State contribution has 
been kept at only 10% as compared to 40% in other States. The basic issue which 
hampers release of funds to the States, including NER States is non-utilization of the 
funds released earlier. Besides writi ng to the States regularly, the Central Level 
Monitoring Committee of the Department of Justice also held bi -monthly meetings 
on regular basis with the States/UTs during which, all the States and UTs were urged 
to utilize the unspent balance available with them expeditiously.

2.14 FINALIZATION OF MEMORANDA OF PROCEDURE (MOP) FOR 
APPOINTMENTOF SC/HC JUDGES :- 
 
2.14(a)  The Committee observes that the Supreme Court and the 
Government have failed to reach a consensus on revision of the Memorandum of 
Procedure (MOP) for appointment of Judges to the constitutional courts, though the 
same is under consideration of both for about seven years now. The Committee 
expects the Government and the Judiciary to weed out their differences and to 
finalize the revised MOP, which is more efficient and transparent, in terms of the 
Supreme Court observation cited above.         (Para 1.58) 
 
Action Taken 
2.15 Hon‟ble Supreme Court while hearing WP(C) 13 of 2015 in NJAC matter 
issued detailed Order on 16 -12-2015 on supplementing the Memorandum of 
Procedure (MoP) and laid down that Government of India may finalize the 
Memorandum of Procedure by supplementing it in consultation with the Chief Justice 
of India. It was laid down that the Chief Justice of India will take a decision based on 
the unanimous view of the Collegium comprising of four senior most puisne Judges 
of the Supreme Court.  The order stated that the y shall take the following factors into 
consideration such as eligibility criterion, transparency in the appointment process, 
secretariat, complaint mechanism and miscellaneous matter considered appropriate 
for ensuring transparency and accountability incl uding interaction with the 
recommendees, the Collegium of the Supreme Court without sacrificing the 
confidentiality of appointment.         
  
              In pursuance of the above orders, the Government of India, after due 
diligence sent the revised MoP to Hon'ble Chief Justice of India on 22.3.2016 and the 
response of the Supreme Court Collegium on the said revised draft MoP was received 
on 25.05.2016 and 01.07.2016. The views of the Government in response to the 
views of the SCC were conveyed to the Hon ‟ble  CJI on 03.08.2016. Subsequent 

 20 
comments of SCC on the views of Government on the draft MoP were received on 
13.03.2017.   
       
                 Thereafter, the Supreme Court in a judgment dated 04.07.2017 in a Suo -
Motu Contempt proceedings against a  Judge of Calcutta High Court brought out the 
system‟s failure of not providing an appropriate procedure for making assessment of 
the personality of the contemnor at the time of recommending his name for elevation 
as High Court Judge inter-alia highlighting the need to revisit the process of selection 
and appointment of Judges to the Constitutional Courts. The views of the 
Government on the relevant points were conveyed to Supreme Court of India vide 
letter dated 11.07.2017.  
 A two-judges Bench of Supreme Court vide its judgment dated 28.03.2018 in 
Criminal Appeal No. 470 of 2018, brought out deficiencies in the system and 
emphasized the need to improve the process of appointment of Judges to the 
Constitutional Courts.  
 
 In another case, while hearing a matter involving M/s PLR Projects Pvt Ltd. vs 
Mahanadi Coalfield Ltd. and Ors [Transfer Petition (civil) no: 2419 of 2019] 
regarding issue of appointment of High Court Judges, the three -judge Bench of the 
Supreme Court, vide order dated 20.04.2021, laid down  additional timelines in 
respect of the time taken by the Government in processing the proposal for 
appointment of Judges of High Courts. However, these timelines are not yet a part of 
MoP. 
  
 The Supreme Court, while hearing another case  No. WP(C) 1236 o f 2019 on 
the matter of appointment of retired judges at sittings of High Courts under Article 
224A of the Constitution of India, vide its judgment dated 20.04.2021 has laid down 
fresh criterion for their appointment. After detailed deliberation, Governmen t has 
submitted its views to the Chief Justice of India on 18.08.2021 to supplement para 
24 of existing MoP which provides for the appointment of retired judges at the 
sitting of High Courts under Article 224A. The issue is still under consideration of 
the Supreme Court. While sending the proposal for supplementation of MoP on the 
criteria fixed in Supreme Court order dated 16.12.2015 in W.P.(C) 13 of 2015 in 
NJAC matter, Government has made suggestions including the need for a Screening-
cum-Evaluation Committee at the Supreme Court and High Court levels to assist the 
Collegiums of Supreme Court and High Courts, respectively.  It was proposed that 
the Committees may screen and evaluate relevant material on the suitability of the 
prospective candidates and wo uld act as a facilitator. The decision to make 

 21 
recommendations will continue to be exercised by the respective Collegiums of the 
Supreme Court and High Courts. However, the Supreme Court did not agree to set 
up such Committees. 
  
 In its recent communication dated 06.01.2023 to the Chief Justice of India, the 
Government has emphasized the need to finalize the MoP in view of various judicial 
pronouncements and inter-alia suggested that the Search-cum-Evaluation Committee 
in respect of appointment of Judges in the Supreme Court and Chief Justices of High 
Courts should consist of a representative nominated by Government of India. 
 
 As mentioned above, the Supreme Court orders dated 16/12/2015 lays down 
that the Government may finalize the Memorandum of Procedu re (MoP) by 
supplementing it in consultation with the Chief Justice of India. Government of India 
has been sending requests to the Supreme Court of India to send its views, as stated 
in the above paras. 
 
 In view of above, it would be seen that the Governm ent has been taking 
necessary actions to ensure finalization of MoP and has sent a number of suggestion 
on supplementing the MoP. No action is therefore, pending on part of the 
Government. The Government is dedicated towards finalizing the MoP in order to 
make the appointment process more transparent, objective and efficient.

c. E-Lok Adalats (Virtual / Online Dispute Resolution):- 
 
Each year, thousands of people throng to the Lok Adalats to settle their cases 
that are either pending or at a pre -litigation stage. However, in the scenario of 
pandemic when protocols of public health and social distancing were being followed, 
it was difficult to conduct such  face-to-face settlement of disputes. As most offline 
services remained closed, online services became the need of the hour. In order to 
adapt to these challenges, the Legal Services Authorities innovatively leveraged 
technology and introduced E-Lok Adalats. 
The main objective of the E-Lok Adalats was to improve people‟s accessibility 
to this ADR forum during the pandemic and reduce the burden on courts by settling 
not only the pending cases but also cases which are at the pre -litigation stage. 

 34 
Another objective was to implement a cost effective and time saving mechanism of 
dispute resolution for the effected parties.  
E-Lok Adalat has been conceptualized in a way that it facilitates party 
interaction and the exchange of information, allowing an opportunity to effectively 
solve a dispute. Pre -Lok Adalat sessions are held to identify cases fit for settlement 
and to facilitate settlement between the parties.   
So far, E -Lok Adalats have been organized in 28 States and UTs including 
Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh,  Delhi, Rajasthan, J&K, West Bengal, Manipur, 
Odisha, Uttarakhand,Haryana, Karnataka, Gujarat, Arunachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, 
Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Chandigarh, 
Maharashtra, Punjab, Sikkim, Goa, Tripura, Mizoram, Meghalaya ad Kerala, In total 
4,32,87,428 cases have been taken up and 70,84,125 cases have been disposed of.

included in National and State Lok Adalat.

The concept of Pre -litigation Mediation was introduced in Commercial 
disputes by way of an amendment in 2018 in the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 
(hereinafter as „Act‟).   Section 12A of the Act makes it mandatory for a party to 
exhaust the remedy of mediation by initiating court proceedings under the 
Commercial Courts Act, with limited exception of cases where urgent relief is being 
sought.

3.0  Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for setting up of Fast Track Special 
Courts (FTSC) for trail of cases related to rape and POCSO Act:-  
 
3.1  (a) As per the data provided by the Department, the Committee observes 
that the pace of registration of rape and POCSO Act cases is much more than their 
disposal rate. Resultantly, as on 31.12.2022, more than 3.5 lakh cases of rape and 
POCSO Act are still pending across the country in various courts. Further, being a  
CSS scheme, State's contribution is also required in prescribed share; further, the 
consent of State Governments is also required for setting up of FTSCs in the States. 
Despite repeated requests, interventions at various levels, the Department is still 
awaiting consent from the State Government of West Bengal, which has been 
allocated 123 FTSCs. Also, some other States have not operationalized all the FTSCs 
allocated to them. Besides this, one of the major reasons being non -availability of 
Judicial Officers to man these FTSCs.            (Para 1.43) 
 
3.1 (b)    In view of the above factors which are plaguing the Scheme, the 
Committee, recommends that in addition to establishment of more FTSCs, the 
Department should also study and suggest how systemic improv ement may be 
brought about to overhaul the entire system of FTSCs. The Committee further 
recommends the Department to explore the best practices in other countries where 
FTCs are functional and have been able to dispose of cases in a time bound manner 
and to bring about the required changes in our system to make it more efficient.  
                      (Para 1.44) 
 
Action Taken 

 50 
3.2 (a) Since inception of the scheme, this Department is making all efforts to 
achieve the target to establish 1023 FTSCs. To ach ieve the goal set by the 
Government, various efforts such as Video Conferences, DO letters at the highest 
level of HMLJ to Chief Ministers/ Chief justices and taking up the issue with 
CMs/CJs in conferences held at Delhi and Law Minister‟s Conference at Ke vadia 
have been made. As a result of constant pursuance, West Bengal government has 
given consent for setting up of 07 (seven) exclusively POCSO Fast Track Special 
Courts in the state.  
  
(b) Department of Justice is continuously reviewing the scheme. In addition to in-
house research and data analysis, the Third Party evaluation of the Scheme is also 
being done periodically by an Independent Agency. The latest evaluation of the

suggestions/recommendations made by the Evaluating Agency have been presented 
before Expenditure Finance Committee in the last meeting held on 15.06.2023. The 
suggestions/recommendations made by the Evaluating Agency on the entire system 
of FTSCs along with DoJ‟s comments will be  submitted before the Cabinet for 
approval. 
(c) In order to assess the functioning of these FTSCs, the Department of Justice has 
created a dashboard to record data from the FTCSs functioning in different 
States/UTs. The Data is collated at the High Court l evel and is recorded for

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS 
ON EMPANELMENT OF ADVOCATES FOR UNION OF INDIA 
 
Q.1 What is ‘Panel Counsel’ for Union of India? 
Department of Legal Affairs has been mandated with conduct of litigations on behalf of 
Union of India before various courts / tribunals in India . For this purpose, Department of 
Legal Affairs empanels Advocates for various courts / tribunals in the country generally 
for a period of three years or until further orders, whichever is earlier. There are several 
categories (court -wise) in which this De partment empanels Advocates and such 
empanelled Advocates are collectively called as „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India.  
However, „Panel Counsel‟ is not a civil post and as such they are not regular Government 
Servant.

Q.4 What emoluments are paid to ‘Panel Counsel’? 
 
As „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India are not Government Servant, they are not paid 
salaries and allowances. They are paid professional fee on case to case basis in lieu of 
their services as per the fee schedule applicable to their panel category. However,  there 
are a few categories of „Panel Counsel‟ which are paid retainership fee on monthly basis 
throughout their term in the entitled category. The fee schedule in this regard is as per 
this Department‟s OM No. 26(1)/2014-Judl. dated 01.10.2015 to be read with other OMs 
containing detailed terms & conditions applicable to „Panel Counsel‟.

Q.5 What is procedure for allotment of cases to ‘Panel Counsel’? 
  
Except in the Supreme Court of India, in all other courts / tribunals, allotment of cases to 
Panel Counsel is made by the Litigation In -charge of court concerned. The Litigation In -
charges have  been decided by the Department of Legal Affairs in OM No. J -
12017/1/2019-Judicial dated 21.10.2019. While in Supreme Court, Ld. Attorney General 
for India selects cases for his own  appearance while other cases are marked by the Ld. 
Solicitor General of India to Additional Solicitors General of India and Panel Counsel 
vide OM No. J-12017/1/2022-Judicial dated 13.09.2022.  
 
Q.6 Is there any sanctioned strength of Panel Counsel (Court-wise)? 
As stated earlier „Panel Counsel‟ for Union of India is not a civil post hence, the concept 
of sanctioned strength is not applicable in case of „Panel Counsel‟. Advocates a re 
empanelled for a particular court / tribunal by Department of Legal Affairs in numbers as 
required from time to time.

Panel Counsel for Union of India may continue their private practice but with restriction

STAFF STRENGTH IN THE DEPARTMENT 
 
Recommendation/observation  
 
2.0 The Department of Legal Affairs has been functioning with about 50% of the sanctioned 
strength for quite a long time, across its grades. The Department has admitted that the shortage of 
manpower for such long duration is affecting their smooth functioning. The Committee has been 
for long; in almost every DFG reports, is recommending the Dep artment to take remedial actions 
to get rid of this perennial shortage of manpower in the Department. (3.10) 
2.1 The ILS, which is the mainstay of the Department and whose cadre control rests with the 
Department itself, has a vacancy of above 50%. The Depa rtment has further informed that they 
have initiated reforming the RRs of the cadre and vacancies will be filled thereafter. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Department to complete the revision of the RRs, at the 
earliest and start filling up of th e vacant position in a dedicated manner. Further, the RRs should 
be revised in such a way so as to avoid possibility of future litigations, as litigations have been 
one of the reasons for vacancies remaining unfilled. The eligibility conditions and career 
prospects in the ILS should be framed in such a manner, that it attracts the best and the brightest 
candidates from the market. (3.11) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 Indian Legal Service (ILS) is an organized Group -A Service, which is governed by the 
Indian Legal Serv ice Rules, 1957. A cadre review of this service is under process, which is the 
first cadre review since this service came into being in 1957. 
 
2.3        In its various meetings, the Cadre Review Committee (CRC) of the Department of 
Personnel & Training di scussed proposals of Department of Legal Affairs, which include 
improving flexibility in allocation of Indian Legal Service (ILS) officers to various Ministries 
and Departments, issue related to provision of reserves in the ILS cadre, merger of the cadre o f 
ILS to facilitate requirement based horizontal mobility and career progression, creation of posts 
above the SAG level, change in existing sanctioned strength (cadre wise) of ILS cadre as well as 
change in method of recruitment in ILS cadre. This cadre re view will help in mitigating potential 
legal disputes in the service as well as enhancing the overall efficiency and fairness of the 
recruitment process of ILS cadre. 
 
2.4.         These recommendations of CRC is under consideration of the Government and is 
expected to be finalized shortly.

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE 
DEPARTMENT AND REITERATES ITS RECOMMENDATIONS 
Overall Assessment of the Demands for Grants 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 From the submission of the Institute and analysis of the functioning of the ILI over the 
years, the Committee is constrained to observe that a premier institution founded for promoting 
and conducting legal research is becomin g insignificant day-by-day due to lack of funding from 
the Government. Faculty positions are remaining vacant, basic renovation and upkeep of the 
institution are held up due to lack of funds. Only a skeletal faculty/staff are maintained with the 
limited grants provided by the Government. As we don't have many institutions in the country 
for legal research and thus, the Government should maintain this institution and not let it die a 
slow death. The Committee wants to see the Institute to become a centre of excellence in the 
field of legal research, for which it requires the support of the Government. However, the 
Committee feels that if the Government is not in a position to maintain this institute, it is better 
to hand it over to some other institutions like Supreme Court of India or BCI etc., like they did in 
case of Institute of Constitutional & Parliamentary Studies (ICPS) which was handed over to the 
Lok Sabha Secretariat. (2.15) 
Action Taken  
3.1 The Department of Legal Affairs provides recurring Grants -in-Aid to the Indian Law 
Institute (ILI) for salary and general purposes. The Department also provides Grants -in-Aid to 
ILI for special purpose, whenever it was required. The Department released Rs. 6.50 crore to ILI 
as special Grants-in-Aid for payment of property tax in the Financial Year 2021 -22 and Rs.1.00 
crore to ILI as additional Grants -in-Aid for payment of arrears of salary to employees of ILI on 
implementation of the recommendations of the 7 th CPC in the Financial Year 2018 -19. The 
Department has also increased the Grants -in-Aid „salary‟ of ILI by Rs.3.00 crore i.e. Rs.3.00 
crore in BE -2022-23 to Rs.6.00 crore in RE -2022-23. The Department of Legal Affairs has 
provided financial supports as well as administrative support to ILI, whenever they required.  
3.2 ILI has also shared their views on merger of ILI with either the Supreme Court of India 
or the Bar Council of India and stated that the ILI has been functioning effectively under the 
aegis of the Ministry of Law and Justice. ILI has also, therefore, opined that looking to the 
distinct and unique nature and work scope of the Indian Law Institute, it is not viable to merge it 
with either the Supreme Court of India or the Bar Council of India. 
3.3Therefore, it would be appropriate if the ILI continues to maintain its independent existence 
with the financial support of the Department and functions under the aegis of the Ministry of 
Law and Justice. The Department has from time to time accepted mo st of the requests of ILI for 
financial and administrative support.  

 
21 
Further Observation  
3.4 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. Indian Law Institute (ILI) was 
founded in 1956 primarily with the objective of promoting and conducting legal 
research. The Committee observes that either the fund or Grants -in-Aid provided by the 
Department is not sufficient to cater to its basic needs like proper infrastructure, filling up 
of faculty positions and other Academic and Non-Academic activities. The Committee notes 
that even after 60 years of its establishment a premier institute like ILI is struggling to 
cater to meet its essential requirements. The Committee wishes to see ILI as a centre of 
excellence in the field of legal research and therefore strongly recommends the Department 
to increase its allocation. 
VACANCIES OF NOTARIES 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.5 On observing the State/UT-wise sanctioned posts of Notaries it can be observed that their 
distribution is quite uneven. For instance for a much bigger state like Uttar Pradesh the 
sanctioned posts for public notaries is 2650 only, whereas for Gujarat, whic h is a comparatively 
much smaller state in terms of population the strength of notaries is 8000. It is also not known 
what criteria are being used to sanction a particular number of notaries in a State. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends the Government to use a fair yardstick and take into account the 
factors like population, litigations etc. while sanctioning the posts of Public Notaries in a 
particular State. (3.19) 
Action Taken 
 
3.6 It is submitted that the number of vacancies for Central Government Notaries in the State 
of Uttar Pradesh was inadvertently mentioned as 2650 and the correct figure is 5150, which was 
increased vide Notification G.S.R. 746(E) dated 18th October, 2021. Further, the vacancies in 
the state are increased in accordance with the number of applications received for appointment of 
Notaries for the particular state.  
 
Further observation  
 
3.7 The Committee is of the view that increasing the vacancies in accordance with the 
number of applications received is not a good criterion to decide vacancies for appointment 
of notaries. The Committee desires that the sanctioned strength of notaries in a particular 
state should be determined only on the basis of its population, number of litigation, 
economic and commercial activit ies in that state, etc., and it should  also be reviewed 
regularly.

VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.8 The Panel Counsels are engaged all over the Country by the Central Government to 
conduct litigations before the High Courts/Tribunals and other courts. They bear the major 
burden of litigations against the Central Government. From the submissions made by t he 
Department, it is observed that the fees paid to these counsels are very meagre, which is much 
below the market rates. The last revision of their fees was done about 7 years back. Accordingly, 
the Committee recommends the Department to revise the fees p aid to the panel lawyers suitably, 
considering the current market rates, so that they remain interested and committed in their jobs. 
It will also help in attracting competent lawyers for being empanelled as a panel lawyer for the 
Central Government. (3.23)  
Action Taken 
3.9 Presently there are more than 6000 panel counsels before various Courts across the

Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.0 The Committee observes that allocations for „Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs)‟ 
has been drastically reduced in BE (2023 -24) over the projections made to the Ministry of 
Finance, by about 90% under the head „Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs)‟. The Co m-
mittee is not aware about the reasons for this maj or reduction. The Committee feels it may be 
due to inaccurate projection or inflation of funds required which is a failure of the Depar t-
ment/ECI, hence this huge reduction. The Committee is therefore of the view that while ma k-
ing projections to the Ministr y of Finance in future, the Department should ensure that its 
projections are rational and appropriate to meet its requirements. (Para 2.22) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.1 Legislative Department is concerned with the Elections related expenditure including 
cases of settlement of Election Accounts of all States/UTs of India, which contains following 
steps: 
• For the purpose, Governments of States/UTs concerned, forward the valid Audit Ce r-
tificates obtained from the Accountant General (AG) offices concerned of the Stat e Govern-
ment, to Legislative Department, conveying the election expenditure incurred by that 
State/UT in a particular financial year, under the Major Head 2015- Elections.  
• Subsequently, all the records/ Audit Certificates are thoroughly scrutinized in t he De-
partment and the dues of Government of India‟ share for that particular financial year is se t-
tled and conveyed to the Government of State/UT concerned, along with the Election Co m-
mission of India. 
• Based on the settlement of dues of Government of Ind ia‟ share for a financial year in 
respect of States/UTs from where Audit Certificates have been received, projections of total 
dues is made at in R.E stage to Ministry of Finance (MOF).  
• After receipt of the amount in R.E. stage, the same is distributed among the State/UT 
concerned. 
1.2 On the basis of above procedure, in the year 2022 -23, Election accounts of 11 States 
(viz. Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Mah a-
rashtra, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tamil Nadu and West Be ngal) have been settled till 27.02.2022 
on the basis of Audit Certificates received from their respective AG Offices. Accordingly, a 
demand of Rs.3166.08 Crore was made in the second and final batch supplementary from 
Ministry of Finance. Subsequently, an amount of Rs.3166.08 crore has been received for 
Major Head-2015 (Elections) in the Second and Final Batch Supplementary.  Thereafter, 
the amount of Rs. 3166.08 crore has been released to the aforesaid 11 State Governments.   

pg. 9

of Finance under the Major Head-2015- „Elections (Reimbursement to State/UTs)‟. However, 
the amount has been drastically reduced by the Ministry of Finance. 
1.4 Further, as recommended by the Committee, in future the Legislative Department will 
ensure that its projections to the Ministry of Finance are rational and appropriate to meet its 
requirements.

diligence and as per constitution requirements and legislative framework. However, the 
Committee thinks that currently, all the bills that are being drafted by the Department can be

men/knowledge. For a laymen to understand the bills which are presented to the Parliament is 
very difficult. The Committee therefore, would like to recommend that the bills should be 
drafted in such a simple language so tha t even a common man can also understand about the

Recommendation/Observation 
2.0 The allocation to the Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP) has also increased marginally by 
7.15 percent over  RE(2022-23) and the expenditure incurred by this wing is 72% of 
RE(2022-23) as on 31st January, 2023. The Committee appreciates the department for proper 
utilization of funds. At the same time, the Committee hopes that more number of authorit a-
tive Hindi versions of judgements of Supreme Court and the High Courts will be done in the 
near future. (Para 2.19) 
Action Taken 
2.1 As regards the Committee‟s observation, Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP) has stated 
that it is a wing of Legislative Department, dedicated for promotion and propagation of Hindi 
in the legal field under the mandate of Constitution of India (Article 351), recommendations 
of Parliamentary Committee on Official Language and Orders of Hon‟ble President of India. 
In the year 1958, the Committee of Parliament on Official Languages recommended that ar-
rangements be made to bring out authorised Hindi version of all reportable judgements of the 
Supreme Court of India and various High Courts for the purpose of promotion and propaga-
tion of Hindi in the legal field and this work should be entrusted to a Central Office under the 
supervision of Law Ministry. Thereafter, on the recommendations of the Hindi Advisory 
Committee, a “Journal Wing” was set up in the Legislative Department in the year 1968 with 
the object of promoting Hindi in the legal field which was later on known as “VIDHI SA-
HITYA PRAKASHAN”. Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan has published Hindi text of about fifty 
thousand judgements passed by Hon‟ble Supreme Court, various High Courts and Privy

REPORT
CHAPTER–I
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS
FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the coordinating agency of
the Central Government in personnel related matters especially in respect of the issues concerning
recruitment, training, career development, staff welfare as well as post-retirement dispensation. The
Ministry is also concerned with promotion of responsive, people-oriented, modern administration.
The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely:—
(i) The Department of Personnel and Training;
(ii) The Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare; and
(iii) The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
1.1 The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister assisted by a Minister of
State. All the three Departments of the Ministry function under the charge of Secretary who is
presently assisted by four Additional Secretaries, three Joint Secretaries and other supporting
officers and staff. The Ministry is divided into seven Divisions, each of which is headed by an
officer of the level of Joint Secretary or above. The Divisions are:
(i) Establishment Officer;
(ii) Services and Vigilance;
(iii) Establishment;
(iv) Administrative Tribunal and Administration;
(v) Training;
(vi) Pension and Central Services; and
(vii) Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
1.2 The Ministry has under its administrative control four attached offices, namely:
(i) Staff Selection Commission (SSC);
(ii) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM);
(iii) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie; and
(iv) Central Bureau of Investigation.
1.3 The other offices under the administrative control of the Ministry are:
(i) Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), a constitutional body;
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), a statutory body;
(iii) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT), a statutory quasi-judicial body; and
(iv) Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB), a body set up by a resolution of the
Central Government.

2
1.4 The Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for four registered societies
set up for the welfare of Government employees and their families. These societies are:—
(i) The Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board;
(ii) Grih Kalyan Kendra;
(iii) Kendriya Bhandar; and
(iv) Civil Services Officers Institute.
1.5 The Demands for Grants (2006-07) of the Ministry have been presented to Parliament under
the following Demand numbers:—
Demand No. 69: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions — Rs. 345.30 crore.
Demand No. 76: Union Public Service Commission — Rs. 59.99 crore.
1.6 The Non-Plan and Plan, Revenue and Capital and Charged and V oted break-up of the total
budgetary projections of the Ministry for the year 2006-07 are as given in the following table:—

DEMAND NO. 76 (UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION)
1.16 The Union Public Service Commission is a Constitutional body, created under Article 315
of the Constitution. The Commission’s charter of duties is given in Articles 320 and 321 of the
Constitution. In brief, it is the duty of the Commission to conduct examinations for appointment
to services of the Union and to advise Government on all matters relating to framing of recruitment
rules, method of recruitment and the principles to be followed in making promotions and transfers
from one service to another. The Commission is also required to be consulted in respect of
disciplinary matters affecting a civil servant including appeals and memoranda filed by individual
Government servants.
1.17 Article 322 of the Constitution envisages, inter-alia, that the expenses of the UPSC
including salaries, allowances and pensions payable to members and staff of the Commission shall
be ‘charged’ on the Consolidated Fund of India.
